title: Albanese evasive over Point Piper dinner attendance
text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has attempted to skirt questions about his attendance at a dinner hosted by a billionaire family accused of funnelling money from China, saying he attends "a lot of dinners".

Earlier in the week, reports by Nine newspapers revealed Mr Albanese had attended the dinner at the mansion of 25-year-old Felix Lee in Point Piper, Sydney.

Mr Lee's father, Phillip Dong Fang Lee, faces allegations of deceiving the Australian Tax Office (ATO) about his holdings in order to channel huge sums into Australian bank accounts.

Speaking to the ABC's Insiders on Sunday morning, Mr Albanese evaded directly referring to the dinner, stating he attends "a lot".

Pressed on his inability to answer, he said, "You just said that that occurred."

"I attend lots of dinners in lots of places, and I don't talk about private dinners," he added.

Election laws would have blocked millions from Climate 200 Climate 200 would have been blocked from making $8.34 million in donations to independent candidates if new election donation laws were in place at the 2025 poll.

Other prominent figures were reportedly in attendance, including Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn and former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews.

Mr Albanese said he was not aware of the money funnelling concerns surrounding Mr Lee senior.

Mr Lee and his wife, Ziaobei Shi, are not new to scrutiny. The ATO pursued the pair for $273 million in unpaid taxes in 2021, freezing their assets before reportedly settling the following year.

"He wasn't there … I attend a lot of meetings, functions, with lots of people. I mean talking about people's relatives, even removed from that," Mr Albanese said.

"We declare all of our donations in accordance with the rules, we're transparent about it. I do attend a lot of events and that is part of the process that occurs engaging with people."

It is unclear how much was pledged as a Labor donation for each attendee but The Sydney Morning Herald claims it was $10,000 a head, raising potential concerns of money buying influence in politics.

James Paterson says the prime minister's attendance at any dinner is a matter of public interest. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said who the prime minister dined with was of legitimate public interest, given his position.

"His refusal to answer any questions about this dinner or the source of these funds raises very serious questions about him and his judgement, and it's time that he fronts up," he said on Saturday.

Independent MP David Pocock said "cash for access to our government has to stop".

"It's one of the ways vested interests have an outsized influence on policy, and we see this in real time on everything from taxing gas to minimising gambling harm and banning gambling ads."

On Friday, several frontbenchers were pressed to respond to reports about the dinner and repeatedly referred any issues relating to donations as a "matter for the party".

title: Love story: How Tom and Huma Busby became the perfect duo
text:
When singer Tom Busby and his musical partner Jeremy Marou were wrapping up their first major national tour as Busby Marou in Sydney in 2011, the last thing he expected was to meet the love of his life.

Fifteen years later, Tom and his now-wife Huma are embarking on their own tour of Australia, and they're taking their four children along for the ride.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

Huma: I'm from Houston, Texas, originally. I'd been [in Australia] for about four years, and an Australian friend of mine named Josh wanted to see if we could catch up and go see a band that he managed, which was Tom's band. We met that night and Tom was wearing a blue velvet jacket.

Tom: It was fake [velvet], but I was looking good. It was 2011 and it was the last show of the first big Busby Marou tour. It was a really good, fun time … but I wasn't looking to meet my [future] wife. Me and Huma hung out all weekend and nothing really happened; I still wasn't sure whether she liked me.

Tom and Huma had a long-distance relationship for about a year and a half after they met in Sydney. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

We started talking on Facebook and keeping in contact. Three or four months later, I came back to Sydney and I pulled out the big guns. We were supporting Pete Murray, so I was like, "come backstage," but Huma didn't even know who he was. We started technically seeing each other after that and it was long distance; we dated for about a year and a half.

Rocky road to marriage

Tom: I brought Huma up to Rockhampton. I'm the youngest of eight, so I have all these nieces and nephews and there were about 30 of them there. It was chaos for her, but she was so excited.

It's a big deal to bring anyone back to meet the family. You never bring a girlfriend back unless it's going to be serious.

Huma: Growing up, it was just me and my sister and my mum, so a tiny [family] … but [the Busbys] were the most beautiful, welcoming family and they just took me in.

I felt like I was home from the moment I set foot in that door, but I fell in love with him no matter what straight away. We got engaged after about a year and a half together and married in 2014.

When two becomes six

Huma: When we met, Tom said he wanted eight kids and I was like, "huh?" Then I went to my first Busby Christmas, and I was like, "Oh my God, I could have a million of these kids." Then we had our first kid, Freddy (Winifred), who's beautiful. We were like, "that was tough; maybe we should [only] have one," but we met in the middle and had four.

(Clockwise from far left) Winifred, Marigold, Henrietta and Herbie Busby. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

We've got three girls — Winifred, Marigold and Henrietta — and a boy, Herbert. The eldest is 10 and the youngest is four.

Tom: I was on tour a lot but luckily, I never missed a birth. They're all extremely special and I got to be around a lot, but I was also always leaving to go on tour. It's easier when they're younger, but the older they get … it's hard. Their personalities come out. [I] miss them and most importantly, Huma's working and doing it all on her own.

Taking the family on tour

Huma: We went to America for six weeks last year, for a family holiday and to record Tom's album. That was a big leap because we'd never all been together for six weeks it and was the best time of our life.

Busby Marou portray a 'positive message in reconciliation' The musical duo has previously been apolitical, but feel it's time to speak out.

[In Australia], Tom was playing at these awesome bucket-list gigs like Big Red Bash [in Birdsville], Mundi Mundi [near Broken Hill] or Way Out West [in Winton]. The kids and I would be at home, which is fine, but we always thought we need to take them to some of these places.

Tom: Over the last couple of years, it was like we were single parenting. I would go away and Huma was left with all of it, plus her work. Then she'd go away for work and I'm running the business and doing it all on my own as well; we were becoming ships in the night.

Busby Marou were having a break and I had my first solo album [Rockhampton Hangover] coming out. Getting it off the ground again is like going back to the start of Busby Marou, so we thought, let's travel around in the caravan for a while, build my social media profile and come up with a strategy so I can be a long-term career artist. We're literally just living off my gigs, but we're happier and we're working towards something.

Tom and Huma Busby are embarking on a trip around Australia with their four children. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

Huma: Today was our first day of homeschool with the kids; Tom was working and I was doing that. Life's simple and there's less to think about … it sounds cliche, we have less, but we've got a lot more.

I reckon our bond is stronger already, I definitely feel less tension in the marriage, strangely, because it's probably where you're going to feel the most tense, because you're shoved in this caravan that you're towing.

Tom: What I'm hoping and thinking, when we come back home — in a year, two years — is we'll have stopped racing, or if we are racing, it's for the right reasons and not [because] we're juggling 1,000 things.

I really believe that it needs to be a simpler life back in the real world and this has already brought us closer together. We're sharing the job load and the mental load and all of the loads. I feel like this caravan helps with that; there's not much to do, but you have your own little roles.

title: Emotional day as East Kimberley native title recognised
text:
It was an emotional day for traditional owners on Nganjuwarr country when the Federal Court formally recognised their native title claim to over 900 square kilometres of land and waters in northern Western Australia.

Lucilla Martin was one of about 100 traditional owners who gathered at Pelican's Nest on the Dunham River for Wednesday's on-country hearing.

"I feel so great that I want to jump over this moon, wherever it is, to be free and to do my things," she said.

But the "long journey" to formal recognition was bittersweet.

"Today I had tears for my dad, my sister, my brother and my mum, I had a bit of sadness today," Ms Martin said, reflecting on family members who had passed away.

Lucilla Martin was delighted to see the native title recognised. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

A major milestone

The Nganjuwarr native title claim filed in 2024 area covers 960 kilometres of the East Kimberley.

On Wednesday Federal Court Justice Erin Longbottom awarded claimants exclusive rights over that area, bringing the total native title coverage of the Kimberley to 97 per cent.

The hearing opened with a smoking ceremony. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Kimberley Land Council, which represented the claim group, said the recognition put traditional owners in a stronger negotiating position with Giliwinggin Aboriginal Corporation, now appointed as the prescribed body corporate.

"It gives us an opportunity to have our voices heard and strengthens our rights and interests," deputy chief executive Sarah Parriman said.

"If effectively should mean that the government and other interested parties need to come and talk to traditional owners."

Erin Longbottom congratulates the traditional owners. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

A formal framework for resources

One of those interested parties is minerals company Tivan Limited, which is seeking approval to expand its groundwater extraction for its Speewah Project, the largest mining venture on Nganjuwarr country.

Grant Wilson and Raphael Sampi shaking hands at the event. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Executive chairman Grant Wilson welcomed Wednesday's decision, which he said would build on the company's existing partnership with Nganjuwarr traditional owners and the Kimberley Land Council.

"The agreement we entered into at the start still governs our process. In parallel, we've been working towards what's known as an Indigenous Land Use Agreement, and that negotiation is ongoing, expected to conclude in the second half of this year," he said.

"And now we have a negotiating party that's formally recognised as having exclusive possession of native title."

Traditional owner Raphael Sampi said mining could "make our country look ugly", but was keen to engage in talks with Tivan.

"I'm going to talk up for the country, find out what they are doing … whatever they are doing, I'm going to be the one there, talking to them," he said.

title: Gas companies go bust and leave oil rig sitting idle off WA coast
text:
An abandoned oil drilling rig off the coast of Western Australia's Midwest is at the centre of a storm about who pays the clean-up bill after the company that owned it went into administration.

Local fishermen and conservation groups are demanding the federal government take action over the Cliff Head oil platform before crayfishing grounds are put at risk.

Pilot Energy was working with Triangle Energy to repurpose the rig, which sits 11 kilometres off the coast of Dongara, about 350 kilometres north of Perth.

But in July both companies, which had a combined value of about $9 million, went bust, leaving a decommissioning bill of $200 million.

Cray fisher Mike Butcher worries what will now happen to the unused Cliff Head platform sitting idly at sea. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Platform 'mothballed'

Dongara cray fisherman Michael Butcher said connection to the coast was one of the most sacred things to residents.

"I'd say fishing is pretty much the most important thing in Dongara, or just the ocean in general," he said.

"It's the main industry in town. [The ocean] is definitely part of our culture."

Mr Butcher, who fishes near the rig regularly, said he had not noticed anyone maintaining the platform recently.

According to local fishers, the aging, ocean-worn Cliff Head platform is falling into neglect. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"There's no-one coming out here on a daily basis checking on it [the platform]," he said.

"You can see for yourself, it's not been very loved or well maintained.

"It's just been mothballed."

Lobster fisher Jonathon Buist, or "Moggy" as he's locally called. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Fellow cray fisherman Jonathon "Moggy" Buist said the area around the platform was home to an "abundance" of marine life and it was important to local businesses that the rig was not left to degrade in the ocean.

"There's an abundance of fish life and caves that rock lobsters live in [near the platform] so it's a really important part of our fishery," Mr Buist said.

" The actual rig doesn't bother me too much because it's a bit of a navigation aid for us, but it's the pipework underneath we'd like to [keep] tidy. "

Crayfish or western rock lobsters can be found in caves near the Cliff Head oil platform. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

'Canary in the coalmine'

In a written statement, federal Resources Minister Madeline King said taxpayers were not expected to foot the decommissioning bill and if needed it would extend an emergency sector-wide levy.

"Titleholders are obligated by Australian law to pay all costs associated with decommissioning," she said.

"In the event of companies being unable to pay I will have no hesitation in extending the Northern Endeavor levy or taking other measures to cover all costs of decommissioning.

" Under no circumstances will taxpayers be left on the hook. "

The Cliff Head platform sits abandoned following the voluntary administration of operators Triangle Energy and Pilot Energy. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Ms King also said the safety regulator would ensure protections were in place for the marine environment.

"The offshore safety regulator has taken a number of steps to ensure the Cliff Head facility does not pose an immediate threat to the marine environment," she said.

But Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said the uncertainty exposed vulnerabilities in the decommissioning system.

"We have $60 billion worth of infrastructure off the coast of WA and this is that canary in the coal mine moment that indicates what else is at risk out there," he said.

"They've [the federal government] talked about having a financial assurances regime. When is that going to be passed and enforced?"

CCWA's Matt Roberts says better systems need to be in place for decommissioning infrastructure at sea. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Concern for other projects

Decommissioning the Cliff Head oil platform was not the only question front of mind for fishers.

Before the company fell into voluntary administration, protests began to stop Pilot Energy testing the surrounding sea bed, home to valuable rock lobster, for oil and gas reserves.

"I'm part of the Dongara against seismic blasting group and that involves a range of people … that are worried about the local environment," Mr Butcher said.

Dongara community members are opposing seismic testing and potential damage to the valuable rock lobster fishery. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The lobby group started in 2025 after Pilot Energy was approved to begin its Eureka 3D Marine Seismic Survey.

Seismic blasting involves releasing a bubble of compressed air that produces low-frequency noise, penetrating rock layers below the surface.

The project, which was set to begin in February this year, was delayed for 12 months after Pilot failed to secure a suitable survey vessel.

With Pilot Energy entering administration, Dongara residents are hoping plans for offshore seismic testing will be abandoned. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Butcher said fishers had been left in the lurch wondering if a project of similar calibre could return.

"We haven't had any consultation from government, [the] National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Enviromental Management Authority, nothing really regarding where we're going in the future," he said.

" But we've got to catch fish so we go to work. "

Pilot Energy administrators Cor Cordis said in a written statement they had begun assessing the rig's future.

"We recognise the strategic importance of the Cliff Head project and will work constructively with all stakeholders … as we assess all the available pathways," they said.

title: 'Bottomless pit of styles' on display at Gold Coast tattoo exhibition
text:
Benji Tobin's career as a tattoo artist began in 1993 with a bottle of liquid courage and a few scribbles on a mate's leg.

"We made a tattoo machine out of an electric shaver [but] my lines were way off and I said, 'Mate, this isn't going to turn out the way we thought,'" he said.

"Unfortunately, all my mates I grew up with have got the worst tattoos I've ever done."

Now Tobin has co-curated an art exhibition called Made to Suit, which reflects how much the art form has transformed since tattoos became mainstream.

"It was the bikies, the crims, the naughty boys," he said.

" Now you can go and get a coffee and the barista has a face tattoo. "

Benji Tobin says there is a huge diversity of styles in the tattooing world. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

'I have to nail this'

Tobin started Made to Suit five years ago as a way to bring the "cliquey" tattoo community together and highlight the vast diversity of styles.

"What I tattoo isn't what I get — what I like and what I get are two different things," he said.

"I'm covered in black and grey but I tattoo in colour."

Dan Johnston with his piece for the Made to Suit exhibition. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

The exhibition recreates more than 30 full-body tattoos on canvas.

Co-curator Dan Johnston submitted his own canvas this year, which demonstrates of how tattoos reflect the artists who draw them.

"After the last Made to Suit, my wife found out she has brain cancer," he said.

(ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Johnston's piece shows 13 samurai-inspired crabs climbing up a body, united in the fight against a symbol of cancer.

"I tried to make it a little bit about a journey that's happening in my life," he said.

"It was personal and I thought, 'I have to nail this and get it out.'"

'A bottomless pit of styles'

Stephanie King says she has seen trends come and go since she started tattooing 14 years ago.

"There's trends at the moment, like the fine lines, sticker ones — I feel like that's boomed," she said.

Stephanie King says the tattoo business is very different to what it once was. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King has built a reputation for creating hyper-realistic black and white tattoos but has changed up her style for Made to Suit.

"You used to walk into a shop and you picked a design off the wall. The people doing the tattoos were probably pretty scary and fitted into a stereotype," she said.

"It's changed quite a bit, there's a lot more women in the industry now."

Tony Nguyen says he feels relaxed when he is under the needle. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King's work in last year's exhibition was found online by New York lawyer Tony Nguyen, who wanted to get a full bodysuit for his first tattoo.

"I was really picky about who my artist was going to be," he said.

"When I first dipped my toe into it, it was a bottomless pit of styles, regions and histories — I got lost in it."

Mr Nguyen said King's art spoke to him so much that he travelled all the way to her Gold Coast studio.

"It was very fluid, there was something not strict, or an airy feel about it," he said.

'A way to tell a story'

It has taken King 12 days to tattoo Mr Nguyen's torso and she has his arms and legs still to go.

But he has no thoughts of turning back.

"It makes me feel at ease. It makes me feel the way I feel inside but it's on my skin and I can see it," Mr Nguyen said.

Stephanie King has been tattooing Tony Nguyen in her Gold Coast studio. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Tobin says people get tattoos for different reasons, but more customers are choosing artists for their distinctive style and giving greater thought to how one tattoo complements the next.

"They don't just go, 'Give me this, give me that' and [I] think, 'Shit, what am I going to do with all this?'" he said.

"They'll come in and go, 'Hey, I like your work, I want to get a sleeve', and that will extend into something bigger."

Lost Woods Tattoo by James Wood is on display at 2026 Made to Suit exhibition. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King said there was more freedom than ever for tattoo artists to be creative and evolve.

"You go for a walk and you see things in nature that inspire you … I love going to galleries and museums," she said.

"People see it as art. It's a way to tell a story."

title: No more tears left to cry as Godwin goes from hell to the mountaintop
text:
Four years ago, Georgia Godwin was at the peak of her powers as she led Australia to silver in the women's team final at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games.

She performed all four of the apparatus and had the highest score in three of them.

This time around, her first two rotations were just OK, aided by brilliant performances by Kate McDonald, whose 14.200 was the best uneven bars score of the day; and Breanna Scott on beam.

They backed it up on the floor, with first Scott, then McDonald posting the day's second-best scores on the apparatus.

Godwin was a picture of composure. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Then Godwin reminded the world of her class with a stunning routine that earned her a 13.350 and left Australia in top spot with only the vault to come.

"There was a lot going through my head before that floor routine and the girls before me absolutely nailed their floors. I just really wanted to help the team and with all of that head noise and all of that pressure I just started feeling a bit overwhelmed," she said.

"So before I started floor, I went to my plans and grounded myself and I was so happy for that to be my first floor routine back at a big international event."

The moment her music faded out, the emotions came rushing into Godwin and out onto her face.

Georgia Godwin burst into tears immediately after her floor routine. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys/PA Images)

Some mixture of pride and relief. Then the tears as she embraced every member of the team who had helped her get back.

The Achilles she tore two and a half years ago hadn't just held up, it had propelled her and her team towards almost certain gold in Glasgow.

Athletes often talk of resilience gained and lessons learned through adversity, but sometimes it just sucks to be unceremoniously kicked off the mountaintop, have your livelihood threatened and independence taken away.

"I'm gonna be completely honest, it's been a horrible, horrible road back," she said.

"My support team has been absolutely amazing, but the mental challenges I've had to go through have been the hardest I've been through in my life.

"But I want to finish this sport on my own terms and I wanted to do one more big event with these amazing girls.

The village got Georgia Godwin through hell. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

"I've said it before and I'll say it over and over again, but it takes a village and I'm so lucky to have my special village."

That village includes her parents, who were in the stands to watch, her teammates, her coaches, physio, trainers, and of course puppy Remy.

Unsurprisingly, there were times when she thought she wouldn't be able to get back.

Too old, too sore, too hard. Just all too much.

It was too much again on Saturday night at the Glasgow International Arena.

The energy was high from the Australians throughout the final. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Asked about her mindset as she stepped onto the floor, the emotions came for her again.

"I'm gonna have no tears left by the end of this," she laughed.

A solid 20 seconds of overwhelm later, she said she wasn't performing for herself but those dozens, hundreds of people who have helped her get back on the mat, the bars, the vault and the floor.

Five seconds later she was laughing about becoming Australia's most decorated female gymnast, and joking at the expense of Allana Slater.

It was another reminder of her ability to compartmentalise, albeit slightly less impressive than when she managed to compose herself after the ultimate release of sticking that floor routine to pull off a similarly superb 13.550 vault.

In a competition where they won gold by 1.1 point, a half misstep or misalignment could have seen the ultimate goal slip through her fingers again.

Georgia Godwin has returned to the top of the world. (Gety Images: Naomi Baker)

"My emotions don't come up very often but when they do I'm very good at suppressing them if I've got a job to do," she said.

"I think it's so important to feel your emotions but there's also a time and place, so I took the moment, got myself into a quiet corner and just laid down and tried to calm myself back down and did the job."

Job done, but not really.

Still ahead of her in Glasgow are gold medal defences in the all-around and vault finals, and a floor final.

But today isn't about any of that.

Today is about reminding her who she is, what she can do, and why she does it.

"I think everything is all good," she said.

"We can move on and I've really taken a step today."

title: Quick hits: Photographer watches partner win gold, tiny nation makes history
text:
The partner of an Australian gold medallist nervously watches his final while working on the pool deck, while a swimmer loses her cap in the middle of a race.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Picture perfect moment

Sam Williamson (right) celebrates with his partner Linnea Lindberg after winning gold. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Spare a thought for Sam Williamson's partner Linnea Lindberg.

As Williamson powered to an emotional victory in the men's 100m breaststroke final, Lindberg was forced to nervously watch on in her professional capacity.

You see, Lindberg is working at the Comm Games as an accredited photographer.

Williamson joked after his final he was not sure about the quality of any snaps she took during his race.

"I can't imagine they'll be good," Williamson joked to the Seven Network.

"I reckon she's got more tears in her eyes than I do at the moment … if we get one good photo from tonight, it's all worth it."

Sam Williamson (left) and Linnea Lindberg caught the eye of poolside photographers. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Williamson and Lindberg were able to catch up and celebrate on the pool deck, much to the delight of the other photographers working at the swimming.

2. Aussie loses swimming cap

Sienna Toohey lost one of her swimming caps during her 100m breaststroke heat. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

No doubt Sienna Toohey thought she was ready for any challenge thrown at her at the Commonwealth Games.

That was until one of her swimming caps fell off mid-race during the heats of the women's 100m breaststroke.

"I got to the end [of my heat] and they [officials] were like, 'Has anyone lost a cap?', and I was like, 'Yeah, that's me,'" Toohey said.

She said officials told her she could dive back in the pool and retrieve the cap, but there was only one problem.

"I couldn't find it anywhere in the pool," Toohey said.

"I was thinking: 'I've got to get this cap back, I need it for tonight.'"

Toohey eventually found the cap, with the Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd giving her a warm round of applause.

The "wardrobe malfunction" did delay the heats program, although no-one seemed bothered.

For the record, Toohey won her heat in a time of 1:07.30.

3. Diamonds put out call to Outlander star

Scottish actor Sam Heughan is in demand. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

The Australian netball team has laid down a challenge to Scottish actor Sam Heughan.

The Diamonds want to meet up with Heughan, who plays Jamie Fraser in the Outlander series, after he was spotted at a Scottish team training session.

Kiera Austin and Courtney Bruce are among the Diamonds players who have taken to Instagram asking Heughan — who featured in the opening ceremony — to come and watch the netball competition.

It seems their wishes may well be granted.

Loading Instagram content

We'll keep you posted on whether a meeting eventuates.

4. McCanns watch son compete

Kate and Gerry McCann watch their son Sean McCann compete in the swimming heats on day two. (Getty Images/SNS Group: Ross MacDonald)

From all reports, Kate and Gerry McCann avoided being accosted when they watched their son, Sean, compete in the men's 400m freestyle at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre.

The McCanns were the centre of a media frenzy when their three-year-old daughter Madeline went missing during a family holiday in Portugal in 2007.

It remains one of the most high-profile international missing-persons cases and is still under investigation.

The parents and Sean's twin sister, Amelie, sat in the stands for both the heats and final.

Sean McCann, who was two when Madeleine disappeared, finished fourth in his heat but snuck into the final, where he placed eighth.

5. Jersey breaks medal drought

Swimmer Filip Nowacki broke through for Jersey with his silver medal. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The nation of Jersey has reason to celebrate after claiming its first Commonwealth Games medal in 36 years.

Filip Nowacki won silver behind Williamson in the men's 100m breaststroke final, beating world record holder Adam Ramsay-Peaty into third place.

"I'm really happy with that swim," the 18-year-old told BBC Jersey.

"It was just a touch outside my personal best, but it's a true privilege racing Adam, the Aussies and the very best in the world in a senior environment."

Nowacki's medal was only the fifth Jersey has won in Commonwealth Games history.

The last medal came at the 1990 Games in Auckland, when Colin Mallett topped the podium in the full-bore rifle.

title: Family shocked by aged care system's complexity demands overhaul
text:
Valma Cupitt is the cherished matriarch of four generations of her family.

But when the 86-year-old's husband and primary carer, Darryl, unexpectedly died in September last year, that family was plunged into crisis.

"It was a crash course for everybody to learn about the aged [care] system [and] to even learn how far Val's condition had progressed," Val's son-in-law Bernard Sheville said.

"We were learning in a hurry."

Val has been living with a dementia diagnosis since 2019, and her husband took devoted care of her for years.

"We didn't realise how much he was taking on, actually," her daughter Michelle Sheville said.

Michelle is the youngest of three sisters and had been working as a teacher, but left her job when she started to care for her mother.

Val Cupitt (third from left) with her daughters Lenore Cupitt, Michelle Sheville, and Cheryl Holberton. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Following their father's death, Michelle, Lenore and Cheryl stepped up to provide round-the-clock care for their mum, which allowed her to remain living in her home.

"It was very taxing and a lot of pressure," Michelle said.

"We had a roster to look after mum, so each one of us would take turns to stay with mum because she required 24/7 care.

"We had no idea how hard it was for a carer," eldest daughter Cheryl Holberton said.

"After four-and-a-half months, it wore us all out," middle daughter Lenore Cupitt said.

Navigating a complex system

While offering Val supported care to remain living in her home, the sisters were also searching for short-term respite care and permanent high care, filling out dozens of highly detailed and unique applications.

It stretched them thin.

"For us it was really a struggle," Michelle said.

" That's when I had to employ [my husband] Bernie as my application secretary because so much was happening. "

It took five months before they were able to secure a room in residential aged care for their mother, and it only happened due to the support of a private aged care broker they engaged.

Michelle and Bernard Sheville worked together to find Val a place in aged care. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

While the family is relieved and grateful, they want to see changes to help other families attempting to navigate the complex care system.

"The system seemed to be set up with the idea that they don't really need to chase the clients, so they don't have to make it easy," Michelle's husband Bernard said.

"Their clients are in desperate need and they can make the process as difficult or as easy as they see fit."

'Cherry-picking clients'

Val's daughters said local free face-to-face navigation support services could give older Australians and their carers more choice and control.

Val with her late husband Darryl in 2024, who was her primary carer in later years. (Supplied)

"We [would] really like to see more navigation services for aged care," Lenore said.

Peak bodies for older Australians agree change is urgently needed.

The Older Persons Advocacy Network (OPAN) helps older Australians and their families navigate the aged care system, understand their rights, and resolve issues with government-funded aged care services.

"Occupancy is sitting around 94 per cent," OPAN chief executive Craig Gear said.

"Which means there is limited choice for people between facilities and we do find that providers are then cherry-picking which clients come in to fit their business or financial model."

Val Cupitt's family hired a private broker to secure her access to an aged care facility. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

OPAN offers free support via phone.

"We do think there should be government funding so that all people can be provided with navigational support to get into residential aged care," Mr Gear said.

"It really shouldn't be up to the provider to take individual applications or, really, importantly to the families, to be going out and I suppose begging for a place in a residential aged care service."

OPAN chief executive Craig Gear says a more streamlined system is urgently needed. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

The national peak body representing older Australians, Council on the Ageing (COTA), agrees.

"They would like to talk to a real person about their particular personal circumstances and how they find their way through the system," COTA Australia chief executive Patricia Sparrow said.

Demand for transparent, universal pathway

In her recent and final public address to the National Press Club, outgoing Inspector-General of Aged Care Natalie Siegel-Brown delivered a sharp warning that Australia is spending its existing $40 billion aged care budget in the wrong places.

Rather than building more residential aged care facilities, she called for the government to reduce demand by focusing on earlier prevention.

Natalie Siegel-Brown used her address to point out serious issues in the aged care system. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"People delay getting help because it is too expensive, others disengage because the system is simply too difficult to navigate," she said.

" By the time people finally receive help, they are dealing with complexity that could have been avoided. "

She argued the problem was not funding, but a matter of value.

"If we are effectively pricing people out of the very care that is designed to keep them independent at home, we are likely pushing them towards something far more expensive to the taxpayer: residential care."

Peak bodies say change needs to happen to give older Australians more choice and control in accessing aged care, while also reducing the burden upon families. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Val's family believes a universal application pathway for all residential aged care facilities is part of the solution.

"It would be great to have one process, one entry point for all the local providers," Bernard said.

"Digital first, but not digital only is really important," Ms Sparrow said.

The peak bodies and Val's family say harnessing technology to provide real-time and publicly available transparency around care vacancies is also needed.

"Transparency would be really great with the whole system [particularly related to] where you are in the system," Cheryl said.

"Otherwise you have no idea where you are."

Val Cupitt (far right) is the matriarch of her family. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Ms Sparrow said Australia already had the means to make these things happen.

"If you think about other things that we all do when we are looking for accommodation or we are getting a ride, we know the technology exists," she said.

" We could make this easier. "

Where to get help:

Carer Gateway: 1800 422 737 Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm

The National Dementia Australia Helpline, for free and confidential support 24/7: 1800 100 500

My Aged Care: 1800 200 422

Services Australia, where you can book to speak face to face with an Aged Care Specialist Officer in person for free: 1800 227 47

Free care finder service for some vulnerable Australians: https://www.myagedcare.gov.au/help-care-finder

The Older Persons Advocacy Network: 1800 700 600 Monday to Friday 8am-8pm and Saturday 10am- 4pm

If you are a carer, you may be able to access support related to aged care navigation from the peak body representing Australia's unpaid carers: carersaustralia.com.au

title: Kids hooked as fishing popularity soars among younger generation
text:
On a cold and windy Saturday morning, the piers behind the Narooma Sports and Game Fishing Club on the New South Wales south coast are bustling with activity.

Despite the challenging conditions, veteran fishers are showing kids how to cast and reel in the snapper and salmon swimming in the waters below.

Ten-year-old Lipo has been obsessed since he first started going out with his dad as a four-year-old, and was able to reel in two fish.

Lipo is either out fishing or at home watching fishing videos on YouTube. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

"I go in the morning because the big fish like to come out during the morning," Lipo said.

" The fight is really fun. You forget about everything and only fight the fish. "

Club vice president Ross Arnold said membership had been booming since the club decided to launch a monthly junior fishing competition last October.

"It's been absolutely amazing. We've got 54 children on our books," he said.

"There's some local, but there's kids who come down here from Canberra and they all participate."

Across the state, fishing clubs say they are seeing an explosion in interest from children eager to pick up the rod and tackle and go fishing.

Narooma Sport and Gamefishing Club has had more than 50 children join its junior fishing competition. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Apps hooking kids on fishing

Stan Konstantaras from the South Sydney Amateur Fishing Association said his local fishing club had more than doubled in size, in part due to the younger generation.

"We've jumped up from 150 members a couple of years ago to 300 plus," he said.

"Seventy-five per cent of that uptake in membership has been kids under 16."

Stan Konstantaras loves seeing children enjoy fishing. (Supplied)

Part of the growth has been fuelled by the club taking competitions digital and having its own fishing club app.

"There's no paperwork, they take photos on their phone, they submit them, they get all the updates on the phone," Mr Konstantaras said.

"As much as we hate technology and mobile phones and social media, when it's used like we're using it, we've seen a huge explosion of juniors joining our club."

Children are taught the essentials about staying safe on the water and the need to wear a life jacket. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Social media trends have played a role, including the rise of FishTok on TikTok showing many teenagers how easy it is to set out and reel in a catch.

But it is not just about bragging rights from bagging the biggest fish, with juniors teaching those younger than them about what they have learnt and where it is safe to fish, while developing a near-encyclopedic knowledge about their catch.

Aspiring fishers are taught to catch and release salmon on the back pier at Narooma Sport and Game Fishing Club. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Mr Konstantaras said it had been so successful for the club's longevity that he was pushing other clubs and tackle shops to embrace the next generation of anglers.

"My local tackle shop guy said the kids are keeping his business running," he said.

The thrill of the catch

While there is no app yet in Narooma, the obsession is palpable in the 17 children who came out for the latest junior competition.

The morning competition includes children who are beginners still learning the basics of water safety and fishing, to the diehards.

Fergus and Archie McCosker go fishing every second day. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Eleven-year-old Archie McCosker was thrilled at bagging a 40-centimetre salmon on the pier in front of his dad Fergus.

"I just enjoy getting to spend time with him and seeing him enjoy something that I like," Mr McCosker said.

At the end, lures and tackle boxes were handed out as prizes, before a heroic number of sausages were consumed in the clubhouse.

Ross Arnold says it is amazing to see so many children interested in fishing. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

While he did not land a fish this time, Mr Arnold said the excitement and enthusiasm on the faces of the children who did was good enough for him.

"They'll fish until they die. That is a skill that they're going to have for life," he said.

"What's more fun, sitting with an iPad or going out and catching a fish?"

title: The 'race against time' to save a nation's precious film collection
text:
They tell the story of Papua New Guinea's rich history and heritage, but culturally significant films from the island nation have been at risk of being lost forever.

"It's a race against time," film archivist Zoe Baru said.

PNG's small National Film Institute (NFI) is located in Goroka in the country's Eastern Highlands and houses a collection of more than 1,300 film reels and tapes.

"Our power supply sometimes is unreliable, so … storage becomes an issue," Ms Baru said.

" With climate change, the place is getting hotter. "

Work is underway to preserve films recorded in the island nation. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

Humid conditions and a history of flooding have created a far from ideal environment for maintaining a fragile film collection.

"When I first started, there were already signs of our film deteriorating and the vinegar syndrome, it was just pungent," Ms Baru said.

Vinegar syndrome is a type of acetate film decay.

An 'urgent' partnership

Enter: the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA).

Using a $200,000 cultural diplomacy grant, the institution partnered with the NFI to preserve the parts of the trove.

Culturally significant films were selected, packed and sent to Australia. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

"It was urgent," NFSA deputy chief executive Jacqui Uhlmann said.

" The collection was at risk, but also the institution was really looking for ways to support their staff in caring for the collection. "

Culturally significant films were selected, packed and sent to Australia, where they were assessed by NFSA staff, cleaned up and digitised.

NFI staff received training in Canberra.

NFSA deputy chief executive Jacqui Uhlmann says the collection is at risk. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

A system, dubbed the Remote Onsite Digital Access (RODA) studio, was specially designed and sent to Goroka.

"What the staff have said to us is that they now have really built an understanding about AV archiving, but that the RODA system, which gives them access to the material on-site, is particularly significant because they can have that ongoing access to the digitised material," Ms Uhlmann said.

'Maintaining memory'

Ms Baru, who is the NFI's only archivist, said the partnership had been transformative.

The digitisation process is slow and painstaking work. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

"We're just so grateful, it just leaves us speechless at times," she said.

" When I first joined the NFI, I only thought that archiving meant to just keep them stored in a cool condition and then just leave them there. "

Challenges remain at the institute, including funding security, and there is plenty more content to digitise.

"It's a forever job," Ms Baru said.

"You have to continuously do things that will help sustain your archives, sustain your collections.

"This collection depends entirely on you and the practices that you set up."

The project involved film carriers being transported to the island. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

While the earliest known moving images from Papua New Guinea date back to the early 1900s, Ms Baru said it was not until the 1970s that residents began holding the cameras themselves.

"For younger people, now that they're exposed to more recent technology, the film archives become a handy tool to them because they are learning through watching and they're hearing their stories from the past," she said.

" You're very emotional when you realise that what you're doing, you're actually maintaining memory for the next generation. "

Telling the story of a nation

A key film preserved during the project was the 1982 movie Tukana-Husat I Asua.

It tells the story of a university dropout caught between modern life and traditional village values.

The film was gifted back to the NFI last year to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Papua New Guinea's independence.

A still taken from footage recorded in Tukana in Papua New Guinea. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

"Every nation has those cultural works that tell the story of that nation, and for Papua New Guinea that was Tukana," Ms Uhlmann said.

The NFSA hopes its partnership with Papua New Guinea could lead to similar projects with other Pacific island nations, especially as climate change poses a growing challenge for audiovisual collections.

"It made me realise how much small interventions like this have big, big cultural impact," Ms Uhlmann said.

"Cultural partnerships can be as impactful as economic partnerships when we talk about building relationships between nations."

title: Victorian Coalition under fire over hospital election pledges
text:
The scale and cost of health service upgrades for regional communities at opposite ends of the state may vary greatly, if the Coalition is successful at this year's state election.

The Victorian Liberal and National parties this week committed to fund a new $850 million hospital in Drouin, in West Gippsland, if elected in November.

The Coalition also recently promised to put $180 million towards redeveloping the Mildura Base Public Hospital, if elected.

A Mildura community campaign group, Build the Base, has asked the Coalition to justify the differences between the election promises.

$570 million of changes

Ahead of the 2022 election, the Victorian Coalition, under then-leader Matthew Guy, promised a new $750 million Mildura Base Public Hospital if it won.

Matthew Guy announced his promise to spend $750 million on a new hospital for Mildura, on April 8, 2022. (ABC News: Richard Crabtree)

In June this year, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson announced plans for a $180 million hospital redevelopment in Mildura.

It would include a 30-bed acute ward, and an expansion of the emergency department by 18 beds.

Referencing the unfulfilled 2022 promise, Ms Wilson said election commitments were "not static" and things changed.

Nationals MP for Mildura Jade Benham said there was "simply less money" to play with compared to 2022.

Jade Benham says there is simply less money to play with now. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

"The needs of the community haven't changed, in fact the population continues to grow, but the innovation and the way that the management and the [hospital] board have adapted to be able to deliver change very, very quickly certainly has," Ms Benham said.

A 'bit of a slap in the face'

Build the Base is a community campaign group pushing for a new or redeveloped Mildura Base Public Hospital.

Upon hearing the news West Gippsland had been promised a new hospital, Build the Base vice-president Stephen Parr said it was "a bit of a slap in the face".

"Clearly the budget conditions haven't changed that much when you're in seats that are closer to Melbourne," Mr Parr said.

"We are one of the most remote hospitals in the state.

Concept art of the state government-commissioned master plan of the Mildura Hospital development was found on the HSPC Health Architects' website in 2025. (Picture: HSPC)

"We have a higher level of complexity and acuity in the cases that come to our hospital because there's no other [public] hospital.

"I would argue that our community needs are higher.

"While there may be need for beds and things down there, this part of the state and our remoteness causes the need for us to have a new hospital.

"We are a very remote part of the state with complex needs, and that's what warrants this significant investment that we're wanting."

The Coalition response

The Victorian Coalition was asked why there was a difference in funding pledge amounts between hospitals in Mildura and West Gippsland.

It was also asked why West Gippsland had been promised a new hospital, while Mildura was promised a hospital redevelopment.

A spokesperson instead directed criticism at Build the Base president, and former member for Mildura, Ali Cupper.

Ali Cupper says the Coalition has abandoned its promise to Mildura. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

"Our team has a plan for the whole state and unlike tried and failed independent MPs — we can actually deliver," the spokesperson said.

"Our $180 million commitment to significantly upgrade Mildura Base Hospital is $180 million more than Ali Cupper ever did, or ever will deliver.

"The only to way to get a better Mildura Base Hospital and ensure our region get its fair share is by backing our Nationals and Liberals team this November."

Ms Cupper made a brief response to the Coalition statement.

"In relation to the personal attack, I'm not taking the bait. Instead, Build the Base will repeat the question: how can the Coalition justify a new hospital to Gippsland while abandoning its promise to Mildura," she said.

The Victorian Labor government spent $2 million on a Mildura hospital master plan in the 2021–22 State Budget, but has not publicly released it, or made a financial commitment to a new hospital, or a hospital redevelopment.

The West Gippsland Hospital received funding for planning and development in the 2023 Victorian budget as part of a $320 million fund to prepare for the delivery of seven major hospital projects across the state.

title: Sobers could only do everything — including for SA's Sheffield Shield side
text:
The cricketer Sir Garfield St Aubrun "Garry" Sobers was a man who frequently found himself the subject of admiration and wonder.

Widely recognised as the game's greatest all-rounder, Sobers — who died recently at the age of 89 — scored 8,032 runs at an average of almost 58, claimed 235 wickets and snared 109 catches in his 93 Test matches for the West Indies.

But even by the time he was recruited by South Australia, as a 25-year-old in 1961, his talent was already indisputable.

"I don't say this lightly — he's the greatest cricketer, in my opinion, the game has ever seen," said Ken "KG" Cunningham, who played alongside Sobers during the latter's three seasons with SA's Sheffield Shield side.

"He opened the bowling, he bowled first change and bowled left arm orthodox, he was second change with left arm [wrist spin], he'd field like a demon and then he could bat.

"He was five cricketers in one."

South Australian sporting legend Ken "KG" Cunningham vividly recalls batting with Sobers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In 1958, Sobers had broken the world record for the highest individual innings when he scored 365 not out against Pakistan in Jamaica — a milestone that stood for more than 35 years.

His arrival in SA the summer after the famous Tied Test series occurred at a time in which there was strong enthusiasm for West Indian cricket.

"It's a little bit murky how it came about, because success always has a million fathers — but it was very much on the back of the 1960/61 West Indies tour, and I think Bradman had a role in it," sportswriter Michael Sexton said of the circumstances that led to SA securing Sobers's services.

"The lure of Bradman was just so important — they got on very well. He used to go and have dinner at Bradman's house in Adelaide."

The front cover of Michael Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers, about Sir Garfield Sobers's time playing for SA. (Supplied)

Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers is a tender tribute to the cricketer's SA seasons and their culmination in Sheffield Shield victory.

There are vignettes from his time at Prospect Cricket Club, where Sobers played at grade level, and the book depicts him in his off-field moments as a man who "charged past midnight, wore out barmen, gambled, chased skirts and lit every scene with the sunshine of possibility that beamed out of him".

Light is also shed on the political setting, and Sexton said South Australian administrators had "to bypass the White Australia Policy" to get Sobers into the squad.

It is an irony of considerable gravity that while Sobers was regarded by fellow cricketers as having reached the summit of their sport, cricket authorities were obliged to seek, with delicacy and discretion, special dispensation to keep him in the country.

'So grateful and so lucky'

In person, there was nothing immediately imposing about Sobers, and little to indicate that his frame concealed an inner Hercules. The short back and sides, the pencil moustache and the V-neck sweater hardly betokened the presence of athletic genius.

But Sobers was, in truth, a cricketer of whom it feels apt to borrow a bon mot: he could only do everything.

The paradoxical presence of the word "only" in that statement adds the crucial note of humility that makes it especially applicable to Sobers, whose accomplishments were usually accompanied by grace.

The news that Sobers was destined for SA generated headlines across Australia. (Supplied)

In one of his six sixes in an over for Nottinghamshire at Swansea in 1968, he performed a complete pirouette, spinning like a sprinkler on a parched outfield.

His bowling action was equally aqueous. The rock back and forward sling prefigured the motions of Jeff Thomson, and the ball was released in a cascade of lithe force.

"He was the best player in the world — and he's just turning up at Prospect to go and have a net with the others, because he was in that team," Sexton said.

"It's an astonishing thing that happened to South Australia. It's probably the equivalent of when Bradman came in the 1930s — it's that sort of impact, isn't it? 'What on Earth is he doing here?'"

For his Prospect teammates, the experience was perhaps not unlike that of an amateur dramatic society that persuades a BAFTA-winning lead to join its players, or a garage band that fills the vacant role of rhythm guitarist by recruiting a rock legend, or a model aeroplane club that without warning is gifted possession of an actual Spitfire.

But Sobers's career in South Australia had unpropitious beginnings, and his initial three outings with the bat for Prospect produced a solitary run.

A team photo of the South Australian 1963/64 Sheffield Shield side, including Ken Cunningham, Neil Hawke, Sir Garfield Sobers, Rex Sellers, Les Favell, Barry Jarman and Ian Chappell. (Supplied)

Even so, his cricketing charisma was palpable, and Cunningham still remembers the first time they batted together for SA.

"I walked down the beautiful steps at Adelaide Oval, onto the oval itself, and went to the striker's end," he said.

"I looked up and I saw Sir Garfield Sobers [at the other end] and I said to myself, 'What in the hell am I doing here? I'm just Ken Cunningham. I shouldn't be here'.

"I was so grateful and so lucky to be able to play with the great man."

Sobers's seasons in SA were like the building and breaking of a wave, and triumph came in 1963/64.

A newspaper advertisement from around the time of Sobers's remarkable achievement in the 1963/64 Sheffield Shield season. (Supplied)

Remarkably, he took more wickets and scored more runs than any player in Australia during the summer.

Among the mainstays of that Shield victory was the bowling partnership Sobers formed with leg-spinner Rex Sellers — the former took 47 wickets, the latter 46.

"I s'pose we might have complemented each other," Sellers reflected.

"He was very accurate, I believe I can say I was pretty accurate as well, so we created good pressure on batsmen from both ends."

In SA's final game — a win against Victoria that guaranteed SA the Shield — Sobers made a century and claimed nine scalps.

"He was pivotal because not only was he the best player, but he inspired the others to play better. He gave them a slight swagger and a confidence that they hadn't had before," Sexton said.

"He lived up to all expectations and hopes."

A tribunal has ruled against national federation Equestrian Australia (EA) after a nearly two-year dispute over one of the Olympic sport’s most coveted prizes. The feud centred around the scoring system used at the 2024 Australian Dressage Championships at the Sydney International Equestrian Centre and divided officials in the exclusive sport. Vivien Lipshut with her horse Estupendo, which no longer competes in dressage. Paul Jeffers The taxpayer-funded peak body fought claims by Victorian horse owner Vivien Lipshut that her imported European gelding Estupendo and his rider David McKinnon were wrongly denied the title of Australian grand prix champion. However, the National Sports Tribunal has found against EA, determining Estupendo and McKinnon the rightful winners after hearing that the scoring format was changed without the knowledge of entrants in the days before the event.

Lipshut alleged she had faced intimidation from one of the sport’s former integrity officers during her bid to have the original result reversed and was vindicated by the decision of tribunal member Anthony Lo Surdo SC. “This was never just about winning a championship. It was about standing up for fairness, accountability, and the integrity of our sport,” Lipshut said. David McKinnon rides Estupendo at the Australian Dressage Championships at Sydney International Equestrian Centre in 2024. Simon Scully “I could not stand by and allow an injustice like this to go unchallenged. If the rules can be ignored in one case, they can be ignored in any case. Every member deserves to know that the rules will be applied fairly and consistently, regardless of who is involved.” Six-time Olympian Mary Hanna and her Paris 2024 reserve horse Ivanhoe 1 were declared the victors after the Australian championships two years ago under on a points system applied by Dressage NSW event organiser Toni Venhaus in the lead-up to competition after consultation with the EA’s Dressage Committee.

Advertisement

But the tribunal determined the scoring change was invalid and against EA’s own rules, concluding that the grand prix champion should have been calculated with the percentage-based model typically deployed in dressage, where horses are judged on their movements during a routine. On that basis, Estupendo and McKinnon would have had the edge. Reacting to the tribunal’s ruling, state organisations Equestrian NSW and Dressage NSW said the championship rug for 2024 would be presented again next month at their awards night. “The decision provides important clarity regarding the application of the rules and reinforces the importance of fairness, consistency and transparency across our sport,” they said. “We extend our sincere congratulations to Viv Lipshut, David McKinnon and Estupendo on being recognised as the 2024 Australian grand prix champion. This is a significant achievement and one that deserves to be celebrated.”

Lipshut, who herself stopped riding after having a stroke in 2017, has accepted an invitation to attend the NSW awards dinner. Related Article Investigation

Equestrian Scoring feud, intimidation claim engulfs Olympics’ most expensive sport But after encountering resistance from national-level officials from the moment she questioned the outcome of the blue riband event, she said the battle had taken its toll. EA opposed the matter being sent to the Australian government’s independent sports umpire, but the tribunal accepted it after an investigation by this masthead. “Although I am grateful this matter has now been resolved, the nearly two-year struggle has come at a considerable personal cost to my health and wellbeing,” Lipshut said.

“My sincere hope is that this determination will help ensure that no member of Equestrian Australia ever has to endure such a prolonged struggle again simply to have their concerns heard.” Equestrian Australia, which will receive $5.7 million in federal funding in 2026-27 via the Australian Sports Commission, has also been embroiled in a legal dispute with its former digital services provider. It has vowed to vigorously defend separate proceedings brought against it by former Olympian Heath Ryan in the NSW Supreme Court. Ryan’s EA membership has been provisionally suspended for more than a year while the International Federation for Equestrian Sports investigates a video that showed him whipping a horse 42 times. Updated WorldEuropeBushfires Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as more than 200,000 people flee flames in France, Spain Caroline Blumberg , Samuel Petrequin and Joseph Wilson Updated July 26, 2026 — 12:44pm ,first published July 25, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Bordeaux/Madrid: Wildfires on the coast of south-western France moved inland towards Bordeaux on Saturday (Paris time), forcing the evacuation of thousands in the city’s suburbs, while blazes over the border in Spain claimed a life. Hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated in both countries. The fires are the latest natural disasters linked to sustained dry spells and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. From a beach in Arcachon, locals and holidaymakers watch in astonishment as the fire rages on the other side of the bay, in Lège-Cap-Ferret. Hans Lucas via AFP “The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X. So far this month, temperatures have averaged 32.2 degrees in the region of France hit by the fires, which is 7.3 degrees above the average July peak between 1961 and 1990, according to data on Reuters Climate Monitor.

Advertisement

“We expect a fight that will be long and very difficult,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters. France’s armed forces have been drafted in to help overwhelmed fire brigades. On Saturday afternoon, an A400M military transport, the largest aircraft in France’s fleet, joined the effort by dumping liquid over a flame-hit forest, as shown in Reuters TV footage filmed from a helicopter. People pose on the beach in Andernos-Les Bains as a fire burns to its north in Lege Cap-Ferret forest, in south-western France. AFP Organisers of the Tour de France announced a truncated 21st and final stage of the famed sporting event, in part to ease the strain on emergency services. In France, as in Spain, smoke billowed from the advancing wall of flames, leaving charred homes in its wake. Three blazes near Madrid, two of which merged on Friday, have prompted Spain to declare its first national emergency over a wildfire.

Advertisement

A far smaller brush fire near coastal Valencia, which began and was extinguished on Saturday, caused the death of an elderly man in his car, the interior ministry said. Spain’s Civil Protection Service said it expected four more water-dumping aircraft to arrive on Saturday, two from Italy and two from Greece – sent as part of a European Union response. Firefighting aircraft from the Netherlands and Portugal have already been deployed. People leave their homes after wildfires in the area forced thousands of tourists to evacuate in Arcachon, France. Getty Images The spreading fires have burned more than 3400 hectares of forest in south-western France. Getty Images High winds have stoked and spread the fires in both countries. The coast near wine region Bordeaux is a tourist hotspot that includes pine forests that can catch fire easily.

Advertisement

Roughly 197,000 people have so far been evacuated from the adjacent Gironde and Landes departments since wildfires broke out last week. In Spain, roughly 88,000 people have been evacuated or confined to their homes because of the three major fires. French minister Nunez said the flames were about 30 kilometres from Bordeaux. The government has warned against road or rail travel to the area. Bordeaux airport remained open, but its website reported train and bus links were affected. “I left without any of my things, with nothing, with the two little children,” 71-year-old Bernadette said of her grandsons after abandoning her house on the coast in the middle of the night. She was speaking at a large conference centre in Bordeaux converted into emergency accommodation. “I forgot plenty of things, my eye medications, everything.”

Many Madrid residents have second homes in the area west of the capital where the two fires merged, which is still in the administrative region of Madrid. Further complicating efforts to control them, one firefighters’ union in Madrid is on strike, although the effect on numbers of firefighters deployed appeared small. Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia reiterated a warning against outdoor activities in Madrid because of the smoke. “Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” she said on X.

Those evacuated near Madrid gave similar accounts of hurried departures to those who sought shelter in Bordeaux. Related Article Heatwave Australia’s used to heatwaves. title: Music Review: Laufey proves jazz music can be cool among Gen Z
text:

NationalWAReview Music Review: Laufey proves jazz music can be cool among Gen Z Indigo Lemay-Conway July 26, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Concert

Laufey

RAC Arena, July 26, 2026

★★★★★

Jazz music is having a revival and has brought with it a new young generation of followers. Thousands of Gen Z fans packed into RAC Arena on Saturday night to see Icelandic singer Laufey perform her A Matter of Time tour – and she did not disappoint. Laufey (pronounced loy-vay) kicked off the Australian and New Zealand leg of her tour in Perth, telling the sold-out crowd she wanted to make the journey to the west coast because she knew what it felt like to live in a place artists rarely visited. Laufey performed at RAC Arena on July 26, 2026. Nicole Mago Foundations Music

Advertisement

“Don’t worry, you guys. I’m from the middle of nowhere. I hope you understand,” she said with a laugh. “So I always feel like I need to go to the places that are far away because I can remember every single artist who came to Iceland growing up, and it was like the most random assortment of artists and I just always felt so seen. “So I just want to thank you so much for inviting me to your country and to your city … you sold this place out, this is crazy there are so many of you here. I really can’t believe my life lately.” The classically trained musician began the show with a selection of her best known hits like Lover Girl, Falling Behind and Too Little Too Late with a live ensemble and four dancers by her side. The castle backdrop, lighting and projections all added to Laufey’s whimsical energy, creating an ambience that felt like something from an old Disney movie.

Advertisement

As an audience member – who is somewhere between a millennial and Gen Z – it was surprising to see how many young people resonated with her older style of music. The show was split into four acts and an encore, and had one act dedicated entirely to jazz. Laufey kicked off her Australian and New Zealand tour in Perth on Saturday night. Nicole Mago Foundations Music Opting to re-invent a handful of songs as jazz pieces, Laufey performed with a stripped back band in a bid to “nerd out” and make the room feel intimate. “With this tour, I really want to find a way to make these very big rooms feel cosy, and I also wanted the opportunity to just nerd out and take some of my older songs and put them in new costumes, rearrange them,” she said.

Advertisement

“So if you’re trying to keep up, and you feel like the beat’s a little funky, it’s a little funky on purpose.” Whether it was because the 28-year-old comes across as a youthful ray of sunshine, or because her music genuinely speaks to people in a way that modern music seems to be lacking, one thing was certain – the younger generation loved it. Two outfit changes later and the performer closed her show with a song called Letter to My 13 Year Old Self. The song was a reminder to never let anyone stop you from becoming who you want to be. In the words overheard by two teens at the end of the song: “I really needed to hear that today.” Pop music isn’t going anywhere, but Laufey is a great reminder that individuality has the power to resonate with people and sell out arenas too.

title: ‘The new LA’: How capital of K-pop catapulted Queensland dancers to stardom
text:
World Street Woman Fighter was broadcast across the globe.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kaea Pearce has danced alongside Jennifer Lopez at the 2020 Super Bowl and stars in Justin Bieber’s Sorry music video, which has been watched more than 3.9 billion times on YouTube. But ask the New Zealand-born, Gold Coast-based performer about the greatest experience of her career so far, and she’ll tell you it was competing on a South Korean dance-battle reality show. “I think it’s the new LA,” Pearce says of South Korea. Last year, she was approached to lead the squad representing Australia on the show World of Street Woman Fighter, a dance competition against all-women teams from the US, South Korea, Japan and New Zealand. Kaea Pearce (right) handpicked the group of dancers who represented Australia. Pearce had just one week to form the AG Squad – a crew of dancers that would be catapulted to stardom among South Korean fans. Her team came second, beaten only by Japan’s Osaka Ojo Gang.

Advertisement

For Pearce, it was the best job she’d ever done. “We were able to be the stars and show the world we aren’t just back-up dancers – we’re artists,” she said. The AG Squad spent time touring South Korea and meeting fans. Instagram @agsquadofficial Brisbane dancer and choreographer Danica McKenzie, also in the AG Squad, was left just as awestruck after her first experience in K-pop. She said South Korean viewers treated the AG Squad like celebrities when they toured after the show aired. “It’s otherworldly,” she said. “Usually [dancers] go to a concert backing up for an artist. No one is there for you. It was insane to know that in Korea as a dancer, you are an artist. You’re an idol to them.”

Advertisement

The Australian dance squad now has a large following in South Korea. Dominique Falla, an associate professor at Griffith University and the author of The K-Pop Content Strategy, said Seoul had become one of the world’s most important centres for commercial choreography. And she agreed that the South Korean attitude towards dancers was hugely different to that in Australia. “[In Australia] you’re a back-up dancer, a body in a music video, and your name rarely appears anywhere,” she said. “There’s very little pathway from skilled dancer to recognised artist.” In South Korea, however, the pop industry places choreography at the centre of musical performance. Dancers “are presented as artists and competitors in their own right”. “The Korean entertainment industry invests in dancers in a way the West simply doesn’t,” Falla said.

Advertisement

The AG Squad in Seoul, South Korea. But while programs such as World of Street Woman Fighter delivered fame to their contestants, Falla warned that sometimes the work was precarious. “Dancers and choreographers can still experience insecure freelance work, demanding schedules, limited bargaining power, and difficulties receiving appropriate credit or ownership of choreography,” Falla said. Danica McKenzie is a performer and choreographer based in Brisbane. McKenzie is a champion for Brisbane’s dance scene, teaching at Mad Dance House in the Brisbane CBD and The Home Base in Darra. But she said she could understand why performers often flocked to Sydney and Melbourne – or further afield – to advance their careers. “There’s minimal opportunities for performers in Brisbane, which I guess is why so many dancers are moving out of Brisbane,” McKenzie said.

Australians may soon struggle to take advantage of free travel insurance policies offered by their premium credit cards, travel agents have warned, as an imminent surcharge ban looks set to hit the generosity of cardholder perks and rewards schemes. The warning from travel agents about the consequences stemming from the reform to Australia’s payments system comes days after ANZ joined NAB and other banks that announced scaled-back credit card rewards programs and complimentary lounge access ahead of the ban on surcharges that have funded benefits and bonus offerings, coming into effect from October 1. Much of the travel-related coverage of the ban has centred on how it will likely become more difficult to accrue Qantas frequent flyer and other airline points and how bonus point sign-up incentives and earn rates on spending will diminish.

Encounter Travel director, travel agent Justine Waddington. “The alternative is that the customer pays by direct deposit, but where some bookings are time-sensitive, waiting for funds to clear can mean the deal vanishes for the traveller.” Only accepting debit “may be my only viable option”, Waddington said. “Just as a customer wants to avoid that fee, so does a business. While the extent of reliance on free travel insurance from their credit cards is unclear, an estimate based on survey data from Money.com.au last year was that 39 per cent of Australians rely on such policies and don’t take out extra paid policies. “Paying credit is the most convenient option for a customer. title: Albanese flags new fuel announcements as petrol prices tipped to spike further
text:
In Brief The Prime Minister said his government was not planning to extend the fuel excise discount past 31 July.

He has indicated there is funding for additional measures but has not said what they are.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government is not planning to extend the fuel excise discount but has foreshadowed there will be further announcements on fuel in the coming days.

The 32 cents a litre fuel excise discount expired 30 June but was extended by another month at 16 cents a litre.

That discount is set to expire 2 August, at which point Australian drivers will no longer be shielded from price increases at the bowser.

Petrol and diesel prices have risen sharply in the past week. In Melbourne, unleaded rose six per cent to $1.80 per litre, while diesel rose 12 per cent to $2.17.

In Sydney, the average regular unleaded petrol price rose 10 cents per litre to 171.5 cents per litre and diesel fuel rose 22.0 cents per litre to 209.2 cents per litre, according to the NRMA.
