Regionally, the NRMA said the average price of unleaded rose 5.7 cents per litre, while diesel went by 17.4 cents per litre.

The NRMA said it expected prices to rise further when the fuel excise discount comes to an end next Sunday, amidst rising wholesale costs.

Global oil prices soared this week, with Brent crude spiking above US$100 a barrel for the first time since May.

Albanese was asked on the ABC's Insiders program whether his government was considering a further extension of the excise discount.

"That's not in our planning at this point in time," the prime minister said, adding that the government would deal with cost of living issues "as they arise".

He said his government had set aside $10 billion dollars for a fuel security plan and hinted that more of this funding was going to be allocated.

"That [the fuel security plan] was about better fuel security going forward, including a government-owned reserve," he said.

"We'll have some more announcements about fuel in the coming days and weeks as well."

He would not say whether these "announcements" related to fuel supply or storage, saying Australians would have to wait for the details.

The statement comes as the ongoing war in the Middle East and the Houthi Rebel blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait continues to create chaos in global energy markets by restricting oil trade.

Around seven per cent of the world's oil output now transits through Bab al-Mandab, off the coast of Yemen. Experts say a blockade there could push prices into the US$120–150 per barrel range— creating further concern for domestic energy supplies.

Albanese said that figures released on Sunday showed fuel usage had "come down" since the US's strikes against Iran sparked a war in the Middle East and led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz early this year.

"It's lower than it was a year ago."

"That’s a good thing ... the longer [the war] goes, the bigger the conflict, the bigger the impact will be.

"This is a war on the other side of the world; we are not protagonists in it, but we are impacted by it, and we’ve consistently called for a de-escalation, and we’ll continue to do so."

According to federal government data, the country has 42 days of petrol, 38 days of diesel and 32 days of jet fuel — all higher stocks than the country had in the March 2026 quarter.

Will raise tariff concerns

Albanese also hit out at the Trump administration's announcement of a new round of trade tariffs on Friday, after it accused Australia of not doing enough on modern slavery.

Many Australian exports to the US will now be subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, replacing a temporary 10 per cent levy that the Trump administration introduced earlier this year.

The prime minister said he would "absolutely" be raising the "unjustified" tariff with his American counterpart.

"We’ll raise it at every level of the Australia-US relationship," he said.

"This will lead to higher costs in the United States and undermine the trading relationship that we have with our US friends."

title: 'It's not just hair': The fight to make curly hair education count
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Veronica Vazquez has always had curly hair, but she hasn't always embraced it.

Growing up in the countryside, she says her curls made her stand out.

"Everyone had straight blonde hair. I remember going to school, getting water from the bubbler and flattening all my hair down because it was just too much," she tells SBS News.

Inheriting her curls from her Spanish father, Vazquez says her mother, who is of Malaysian heritage, didn't have the tools or knowledge to style and manage curly hair.

Now a mother herself, she has watched her nine-year-old daughter, Ivory, who also has curly hair, face the same challenges of standing out among her peers at school.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She says she's determined to break the cycle and empower her daughter to feel confident about her appearance.

Veronica Vazquez is determined to give her daughter the confidence to embrace her curly hair, something she says took her years to learn herself. Source: SBS News

"I just have to embrace, educate and show her all the beautiful styles that are possible with curly hair."

For many Australians with curly, coily and afro-textured hair, finding a hairdresser with the right skills remains a challenge. Stylists say the problem starts in the classroom, where training has long failed to keep pace with the needs of textured hair.

Finding a stylist who understands curls

A horror haircut is a common experience within the curly hair community.

Unlike straight hair, curly, coily, afro or textured hair has a different structure that requires specialised cutting techniques. Experienced stylists often cut textured hair while it is dry to better understand how the curls fall and frame the face.

Vazquez and her daughter travel nearly two hours to Curl Lab in Sydney, a salon specialising in curly hair cuts and education, but she says it took years of trial and error to find the right place.

"We went to one salon, and they straightened Ivory's hair and cut it. Unfortunately, her hair is never straight, so by the time we've gone home, showered, the curls bounced up and it was just chopped everywhere," she says.

It's really no fault of the stylist; they're just not educated in how to cut curly hair.

Curl Lab owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system teaches students the same cutting techniques for clients with both straight and textured or afro hair, rather than providing training tailored to different hair types.

"If you're cutting curly hair when it's straightened or wet, it's going to look good until the curls bounce up," Thandekafountas tells SBS News.

Sydney-based salon owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system fails to tailor cutting techniques to different hair types. Source: SBS News

"We like to call it the 'Lord Farquaad' bob, so many clients come in for us to fix that," referring to the character from the film Shrek, who has a pageboy bob haircut.

How history shaped hair standards

The challenges faced by many people with curly and afro-textured hair are rooted in decades of beauty standards that experts say favoured straight hair.

Early anthropologists and naturalists once used the colour and texture of hair as markers of social hierarchy.

Farida Fozdar, a sociologist and professor of anthropology at Curtin University, says hair texture, much like race, was historically used to reinforce ideas about status, with so-called 'Caucasian hair' — blonde, light coloured or straight hair — often viewed as the ideal.

"There was a bit of a tendency to assume kinky, or curly hair was somehow abnormal or a lesser quality of hair," she tells SBS News.

"There were a number of researchers who described it as 'woolly' hair, suggesting it was more like animals."

Fozdar says those attitudes began to shift as Australia became more culturally diverse following the end of the White Australia policy and the increase in migration from the 1960s onwards.

"People who migrated in the 60s, 70s and 80s found it very difficult to find hair salons, but there is a growing awareness about the need to cater to populations who are different," she says.

While specialist salons are now becoming more common, many stylists say education and training have struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population.

Why hairdressing education is falling short

More than a decade ago, afro and curly hair education became part of the national training curriculum developed by Service and Creative Skills Australia (SaCSA), the Jobs and Skills Council for personal services.

However, the content is delivered as optional training in some qualifications, meaning many apprentice hairdressers can complete their studies with little or no practical experience working with textured hair.

In some states, including NSW, there's an elective unit on using a protein treatment to relax curly hair that teaches professionals to analyse hair, select products, apply heat, and smooth curls.

Amelia Canet, a curl stylist based in Sydney, says the standard hairdressing training qualification doesn't adequately cover the basics.

Many hair stylists say hairdressing and barbering training has struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population. Source: SBS News

"There wasn't any curl education at all. If we did have any textured clients, we were told just blow-dry them," she tells SBS News.

Other curly stylists, like Tulsi Prasad, say they had to take matters into their own hands and teach themselves to cut and style textured hair.

"I just had to learn on my own, watch my own videos, do my own private course, but go through TAFE to learn the proper ways to do everything else," she tells SBS News.

Salon owner Thandekafountas says she invests heavily in training because graduates often arrive without the skills needed to confidently work with textured hair. She sets aside a portion of the business budget to train new staff.

"We need to catch up. Close that gap and really have things mainstreamed," she says.

"How come we're not being serviced in the same way someone with straight hair is?"

It's not just hair; it's our identity, it's our culture, and for so long we've been told that it's too big, it's too busy, it's not professional. So we really want to change that image.

The push for curriculum reform

In March 2025, SaCSA began reviewing and updating its standards for some of the hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs.

Part of its proposal includes recommendations for three new units focusing on cutting and colouring curly and coily hair.

Natalie Turmine, CEO of SaCSA, says learners will also gain knowledge of the history and culture of curly and coily hair, but adds there isn't enough demand in the industry for the units to become compulsory parts of the curriculum.

"As demand and industry become more aware and more customers are coming in and that demand builds, then we'll be able to look at potentially building in skill sets and building it in as a mandatory part of the qualification," she tells SBS News.

SaCSA is undertaking a review of some hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs. Source: SBS News

For the hairdressing industry, the recommendations represent more than just new training units — they signal growing recognition of the need for textured hair education.

Fiona Beamish, CEO of the Australian Hairdressing Council, says the proposed reforms are a significant first step and hopes the units will eventually become compulsory.

"Data tells us that we are ready for this training package to include these units and I'd like to think in the future we could have this as a mandatory training package," she tells SBS News.

Driving change from within the industry

The push for better training comes as the hairdressing industry continues to grapple with a shortage of skilled workers.

According to Jobs and Skills Australia, only 45 per cent of advertised hairdressing roles were filled in 2022-23, with 85 per cent of applicants deemed unsuitable.

A 2026 SaCSA report examining the drivers behind the hairdressing workforce shortage found the sustainability issue is largely linked to "outdated course content and insufficient workforce preparation", raising broader questions about whether current training is meeting the industry's needs.

Sydney hairstylist and educator Chrissy Zemura has spent years delivering private courses and professional education, and creating products for customers with textured hair.

In 2020, she started an online petition calling for a mandatory module on curly and afro-textured hair, which attracted more than 42,000 signatures.

"While the curriculum is the mountain peak, a lot has changed over the past six years, including people's mindsets," Zemura tells SBS News.

SaCSA says the updated training recommendations are in the final stages of review with state and federal departments. They will then be assessed by the Assurance Body before the new training package is published early next year.

title: 'Very volatile stock': A caution to Tesla investors as Musk doubles down on AI
text:
in brief Tesla's profits have dropped after heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on earnings.

Some experts say companies may have to invest heavily in AI to stay competitive in the future.

Financial analysts have warned not to expect much stability in Tesla's share price after CEO Elon Musk defended billions of dollars of investment at the electric vehicle manufacturer, which has just seen one of its worst stock market falls in years.

This week, Tesla reported second-quarter profit of $US1.1 billion ($1.57 billion), down about 5 per cent from a year earlier, as lower vehicle prices and heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on the company's earnings.

The result translated to 33 cents a share, well below analysts' expectations of 53 cents, while revenue rose 26 per cent to $28.2 billion.

Although Tesla beat expectations for second-quarter vehicle deliveries earlier this month, the company said profitability was hit by lower vehicle selling prices, reduced revenue from regulatory credits and unspecified "energy warranty-related charges".

Capital expenditure more than doubled to $5.8 billion ($8.3 billion) during the quarter as Tesla accelerated investment in AI and manufacturing.

Tesla is embarking on a massive construction spree that Musk characterised on a conference call as probably the United States' "fastest industrial scale-up since World War Two".

The company said production of its Cybercab had begun in Texas, the Tesla Semi remained on track for 2026, and subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving driver-assistance program continued to grow.

Asked about scaling Tesla's robotaxi business, Musk said the company was focused on achieving near-perfect reliability.

"How many nines of reliability do you need to scale?" Musk said. "Ideally, you want 99.99999, you know, per cent reliable."

AI investments are 'very expensive'

Tesla's spending has drawn scrutiny from investors concerned about returns on its AI investments.

CFRA Research analyst Garrett Nelson said uncertainty over the spending had weighed on Tesla shares.

"They just haven't been very transparent with [Wall] Street on the expected return of the dollars that have been spent."

Jai Mirchandani, chief executive of Elm Responsible Investments, said the spending reflected Tesla's long-term strategy.

"The company and Musk is saying that it's one of the best investment opportunities and that's why they're investing so heavily in AI and robotics primarily," he told SBS News.

"As we've seen from companies like even Google and Microsoft and all the tech leaders, it's very expensive, and it requires a lot of capital to build the AI infrastructure and technology.

"And if you want to succeed in this space, our view is that you have to be investing in AI and innovation."

Mirchandani described AI as a revolutionary technology that needs "a lot of capital investment".

Musk defends Tesla spending

Musk said Tesla's capital expenditure (capex) was justified, saying the company "should be spending on capex as fast as we can spend ... without it being too wasteful".

"It's OK to be a little less capital efficient if we get things done sooner."

Tesla's chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said research and development costs would "continue to grow in 2026 and beyond".

Speculation has also grown about closer ties between Tesla and SpaceX following the rocket company's stock market debut, although Musk declined to discuss any potential combination.

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

"There's more and more overlap," said Musk.

"Obviously, we can't talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It's got to be done with the appropriate process."

Mirchandani cautioned investors about Tesla's share price movements.

"The reality is that Tesla is a very volatile stock. And so I'd sort of just be mindful of that."

Watch and see

Stockbroker Richard Hemming said investors were increasingly rewarding companies that continued to innovate.

"I think the innovation part of it is more worrying for investors for companies that don't innovate," he told SBS News.

"I think that, in the next reporting season, it's going to be interesting to see how companies ... are going in the sales line. "

He said Australia's upcoming corporate reporting season would provide an important test of company profitability.

"We are seeing sort of signs, especially in Australia, that productivity's falling," he said.

"Productivity in Australia has been under a lot of pressure versus the rest of the world because I guess we're not seeing the kind of innovation that they're seeing in the US.

"So definitely, the upcoming results are going to be very, very important. "

title: The momentary slip that only showed Albanese's escalating control of the Labor Party
text:
IN BRIEF The 50th national conference of the Australian Labor Party was held in Adelaide over the last few days.

The conference was almost entirely devoid of the passionate and public policy brawls once seen at such events.

"We are proudly a progressive movement: two words that can't be applied to the escalator in this building," Anthony Albanese said to much mirth at Friday's Labor Party conference dinner.

The viral moment — in which the prime minister's descent came to a sudden, jolting stop, followed by an expletive-laden reaction — was one of the very few times this week that the veteran Labor party animal didn't appear to have a level of mastery over events that unfolded in Adelaide at Labor's once-a-term policy palooza.

With his gag lapped up by the crowd of party faithful, many of whom paid a door charge of $135 to attend the gala dinner, Albanese continued:

"When it [the escalator] did come to a standstill, I'll admit there was a moment, just a moment, when the ladder of opportunity finally made sense," he said, riffing on former leader Mark Latham's ill-fated slogan from 2004, one of the party's more recent political low-points.

Two decades on, having achieved Labor's most powerful parliamentary majority in history, the prime minister said the party "can finally laugh about making him leader".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While the glow may have dimmed in the wider electorate, judging by recent polling, Albanese seemingly retained the halo of that 2025 election result among the delegates who 'debated' the party's platform this week.

The conference's myriad factions moved deftly to almost entirely avoid the passionate and public policy brawls of the past, which Albanese, the apex predator of the Labor left, used to once involve himself in.

VAD motion sees rare moment of debate

All but one of the various amendments and motions was passed with unanimous support on the floor.

The sole outlier, a commitment for the government to remove barriers around using telehealth to access voluntary assisted dying (VAD), allowed a sole delegate to speak against the motion, the sole amendment to pass where some delegates voted against.

The party also enshrined in its constitution a conscience vote for MPs on this issue, similar to that allowed on abortion.

Trade Minister Don Farrell — a longtime Labor right power-broker who remains opposed to euthanasia — rejected suggestions debate was being suppressed among delegates.

"Far from a graveyard, this is a flowering of democracy," Farrell told the floor on Saturday to much applause.

Husic's Gaza resolution dropped

Backbench MP Ed Husic had a far more pessimistic assessment, arguing that a perception has formed among Labor MPs that "taking a different stand or taking different ground presents a risk to the stability of government".

The former industry minister has found liberation in his backbench demotion by fashioning himself as a rebel with no shortage of causes.

Beyond his well-known divergences with party colleagues on Israel and Gaza, he's also pushed for a new gas tax and a rethink of AUKUS.

On Friday, he called for the government to implement the outstanding elements of the Uluru Statement from the Heart.

But despite claiming some credit for the government's decision to recognise Palestinian statehood last year, his advocacy this year ultimately led to nought in Adelaide.

He cut a lone, isolated figure on Saturday morning roaming the cavernous halls of the Adelaide Convention Centre, as he learned he'd lost the support he required to put up a rival resolution on the Gaza war.

"You've got to be able to find a way to disagree respectfully and try and work with people and have that discussion," Husic told journalists shortly after it became clear his support had evaporated.

READ MORE UN accuses Hamas of hampering aid as EU pledges billions to rebuild Gaza

Husic's resolution, as seen by this correspondent, was ambitious in its language.

It called on Labor's platform to acknowledge a 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that Israel's legal actions in the West Bank breach International conventions on apartheid, and that the party expressed alarm over the UN independent commission of inquiry's findings of Israeli-conducted genocide against Palestinians — both of which Israel refutes.

The resolution also advocated a ramp-up in sanctions on Israel, the prosecution of dual nationals alleged to have committed war crimes with the Israeli military, and for the government to withdraw defence co-operation and diplomatic personnel from the Australian embassy in Tel Aviv.

The chance of it being allowed to go to a debate seems even more remote, given the criticism expressed by other groups, including the Israeli embassy, that the draft platform had been too soft on Hamas, having omitted a call for the group to disarm from the wording.

In the conference's fringe area, where the panels among punters presented far more of an ideological contest than the conference floor, a booth set aside for Labor Friends of Israel was left empty on the event's opening day, and removed by the weekend.

"To be able to have those discussions is a sign of strength, not a sign of weakness," the Western Sydney MP said, mimicking one of the prime minister's favourite bits of Medicare stage play by flaunting his own Labor membership card.

"They can put me in the freezer, I don't give a sh-t."

Jewish-Palestinian duo support current position

Husic's hastily called press conference clashed with the start of the foreign policy debate, meaning he walked onto the floor midway through back-to-back speeches from Jewish MP Josh Burns and Palestinian Australian MP Basem Abdo in support of the unamended foreign policy platform.

Burns said both he and Abdo were "fathers who dream of taking their children to a land free from conflict" and spoke positively of the solidarity shared by his colleague in the aftermath of the Bondi terror attack, as well as the importance of recognising the pain of others.

Abdo, who since being elected in 2025 has kept a low profile in parliament on the war, spoke about the occupation experienced by generations of Palestinians, conceding "no single motion can do justice" to the challenges experienced in recent years by both of their communities.

READ MORE Israeli troops shoot dead seven-month-old Palestinian baby in the occupied West Bank

The Albanese-era Labor Party has ultimately been successful in making this conference a showcase of unity in purpose, with any show of dissent successfully cauterised by the countless closed-door discussions between Labor's myriad factions, away from the cameras of the substantial media pack.

It makes the passionate on-stage embrace between Burns and Abdo, which merited a lengthy standing ovation, stand out even more.

title: 2026 Census Australia: Key dates, what's included and why it matters
text:
Every five years, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) counts every person and every household in the country as part of the Census of Population and Housing.

That includes Australians, young and old, from metropolitan and rural Australia. Even holidaymakers, international students and temporary visa holders are counted on Census night. It's often referred to as the most comprehensive snapshot of Australia, akin to a family photograph of the country.

This year, the Census will take place on Tuesday 11 August.

Emily Walter, Census national spokesperson at the ABS, said it's about more than just numbers. She believes the Census tells a story of a changing Australia.

"Our Census provides a snapshot of the country at a point in time ... So, it's really important that absolutely everyone is reflected in the Census," she told SBS Urdu.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It is compulsory for that very good reason, and it's important that we get a very accurate count of the number of people in Australia ... because it's about providing data for the country to help serve the country."

What the Census measures

The first population count in Australia dates back to 1788. In 1911, the ABS ran its first national Census, with field officers travelling by horse or bicycle to collect information about Australians.

Generally, one person completes the Census form for the entire household. The Census can be completed online or on paper. Credit: Australian Bureau of Statistics

Today, the Census is available online and by paper and can also be completed with help from Census field staff.

It's compulsory for everyone in Australia to complete the Census. Generally, one person from each household completes the Census — although you can ask for separate forms for privacy reasons.

If an Australian is overseas on Census night, they don't need to complete the Census.

The ABS collects personal information about individuals, including age, country of birth, cultural background, living situation, work and education. Some questions about religious affiliation, gender and sexual orientation (for people aged 16 and over) will be optional.

All information collected is confidential and protected by law.

What is Census data used for?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, schools, health care, infrastructure and business. It also helps plan local services for individuals, families and communities.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

The data is often used by researchers to study a range of topics, including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

The 2021 Census counted over 25 million people in Australia, excluding overseas visitors. That was an 8.6 per cent increase compared to 2016. Source: AAP

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census provides an "important suite of information" for decision-makers.

"We've seen internationally what happens when the statistical undertaking of a Census is compromised. That means that we lose vital information, data is unable to be published ... that then leads to policymakers making decisions basically blindfolded, and it especially harms people in minority groups," she said.

She also believes the Census provides the nation with an opportunity to pause and plan for Australia's future.

"The Census for me is not just about data.

"It's about us coming together as a nation, being seen, being captured in that family photograph and ensuring that the future of this country will be data-informed and policy will reflect exactly who we are."

title: 'Life delayed': The $11,710 bill keeping some couples apart
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Bringing a partner to Australia has long been a costly and time-consuming process.

As of this month, applicants now face a record application fee of $11,710 — up $2,345 from the previous charge — while many continue to wait well over a year for a decision, leaving couples separated for months and, in some cases, years.

For Sarosh Akram, the increase came just as he was preparing to apply for his wife's offshore partner visa.

"It's made me think harder about how to save enough to lodge the application sooner, so I can start my wait in the Department [of Home Affairs'] queue," the 32-year-old tells SBS News.

Living in Parkes, a town in the central west of NSW, Akram is now exploring ways to cut costs and grow his savings to cover the additional amount required to apply.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

This has further complicated my situation and delayed my life, which I intended to start with my partner in Australia.

Akram says the fee increase has delayed his plans to lodge the application, adding another hurdle before he and his wife can begin the process of reuniting in Australia.

For Sarosh Akram, the immediate challenge is to find the extra money he now needs to lodge a partner visa application for his wife. Source: Supplied / Sarosh Akram

Akram's case highlights a broader debate over Australia's partner visa system, now among the most expensive in the developed world, with applicants facing rising fees and lengthy waits, while the government argues the increases are needed to fund migration system reforms.

Paying more, waiting longer

Partner visa applications can be lodged through two pathways: offshore for applicants outside Australia and onshore for applicants already in Australia.

Both pathways involve a two-stage process: eligible applicants first receive a temporary partner visa before becoming eligible for permanent residency at a later stage. The full visa application charge (VAC), however, is paid upfront when the combined application is lodged.

According to the Department of Home Affairs' website, the median processing time for offshore partner visa applications is approximately 16 months, meaning half of the applicants receive a decision within that period. Ninety per cent of applicants receive a decision within 27 months. The data was last updated on 26 June 2026.

Source: SBS News

Those waiting times have become a reality for partner visa sponsors like Ahtesham Altaf.

The 36-year-old lodged his wife's offshore partner visa application in January and has been waiting ever since.

"I applied with the hope that I would get a visa soon, as I was paying quite a higher price compared to other visas, but instead I've been waiting since then," he tells SBS News.

I've tried multiple visa options to bring my wife to Australia, but even her visitor visa application was refused.

Working as a civil engineer in the regional NSW city of Maitland, Altaf moved to Australia in 2023 as a skilled migrant on a permanent visa.

He says he has since spent close to $10,500 on visa fees and medical checks, with no certainty about when his wife will be able to join him.

Ahtesham Altaf lodged his wife's offshore partner visa application in January and has been waiting since then. Source: Supplied / Ahtesham Altaf

Abul Rizvi, former deputy secretary of the immigration department, says cases like Altaf's reflect a "growing" backlog that fee increases alone are unlikely to fix.

The fee increases are generally poor policy.

"The fee increase may marginally slow the application rate , but the backlog is so big and the application rate so much higher than the finalisation rate and the planning level that the backlog will keep growing," Rizvi tells SBS News.

He also raises questions about how visa fee revenue is being used.

"The current political climate means the government can increase the fees to extraordinary levels and it appears not to use the money to clear backlogs without fear of political criticism."

What does the government say?

The government says the increase in VAC is part of wider reforms to the migration system and is intended to support improvements across the migration program.

In an interview with SBS Nepali, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he did not accept the way the visa fee increase has been characterised, arguing visa fees needed to be considered alongside other costs involved in moving overseas.

"Just remember with the costs as well, anybody who's travelling overseas for an extended period of time has already decided that they've got the cost of an airfare and, you know, the visa fees are, are well below that," he said.

Credit: SBS

Burke acknowledged the importance of partner visas and the personal circumstances behind many applications, but said the government must make decisions across the entire migration system with available resources.

"Every visa category exists because there are benefits to Australia and the sort of country we are if we can fill those positions. And I have to deal with that with the limited resources that we have."

Among the 'highest-cost' partner visa pathways

Rumina Iqbal, a Melbourne-based registered migration agent who has worked with partner visa applications for the past decade, says applicants are paying significantly more for a process where waiting times have remained broadly similar.

While VACs are typically reviewed and adjusted annually, with changes taking effect from 1 July each year as part of the government's standard indexation process, Iqbal says this year's increases for some visa categories are unprecedented and exceed what would ordinarily be expected from CPI-linked indexation.

Every year, there is an increase in the partner visa fee, but it was never this much. This time, it's huge.

Australia's partner visa cost is among the highest compared with similar family migration pathways in several countries. The United Kingdom's spouse visa, applied for from outside the country, costs about $3,942, while New Zealand's Partner of a New Zealander Resident Visa costs about $4,438.

By comparison, a standard Canadian spousal sponsorship costs about $1,364 in government fees, while the United States pathway costs around $1,872 to 1,955.

The fee varies across countries because some include the medical examination and other miscellaneous charges in the total upfront cost.

Migration agent Rumina Iqbal says partner visa applicants are paying a lot more for a process where waiting times have remained largely similar. Source: Supplied / Rumina Iqbal

While migration systems and eligibility requirements vary between countries, Iqbal says the comparisons show the financial burden faced by Australian partner visa applicants.

"When we look at the price tag, it's one of the highest in the developed world, with such long waiting times," she says.

She says the financial pressure extends beyond the initial payment, as partner visa application fees are generally non-refundable.

"If your relationship ends, then, other than in very limited circumstances, you might not be able to get your visa fee back," she says, noting that family violence and partner death are among the few exceptions.

Iqbal says applicants need to carefully consider the financial commitment before lodging, as the cost can add to the pressure during an already lengthy process.

She says the government could reduce that stress by allowing applicants to split the payment across the visa stages rather than paying the full fee upfront.

The cost of waiting

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said the government is investing in reforming the migration system through the 2026-27 federal budget, with additional revenue from the VAC increases supporting these reforms alongside other priorities.

The spokesperson said Australia remains an attractive destination, and higher application charges are unlikely to materially affect demand for most visa categories.

They say VACs are often only a small part of an applicant's overall cost to travel to, work in, or live in Australia.

"Migrants come to Australia seeking access to our strong labour market, high quality of life, reliable infrastructure, and stable political climate," the spokesperson told SBS News.

The department also notes that demand for permanent visas continues to exceed the places available under Australia's permanent migration planning levels.

For sponsors like Akram, the challenge is finding the extra money needed just to lodge an application.

For others like Altaf, paying the fee was only the beginning. He is still waiting for the decision that will allow his wife to join him in Australia. Until then, the thousands of dollars spent have secured little more than a place in the queue.

title: Flaming teacakes, bedazzled unicorns: The Commonwealth Games' surprises unpacked
text:
In brief The Commonwealth Games has opened in Glasgow, Scotland, with a quirky ceremony.

King Charles and Queen Camilla got in on the act, referencing a famous UK sci-fi TV show.

The Head of the Commonwealth emerging from a time-travelling blue box, unicorns prancing on stage, and fire spurting from an oversized teacake.

Those were the scenes at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Friday morning.

Victoria was initially meant to host the games, but withdrew in 2023 due to soaring costs.

Glasgow, which previously hosted the event in 2014, stepped in to save it — and brought their finest, most-bedazzled unicorns to mark the occasion.

This year's Commonwealth Games is running on a bare-bones budget, arriving at a time when people have questioned their relevance, particularly following the Victorian government's withdrawal.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But despite the troubles, Friday's ceremony was a party — with scenes that looked like they could have been plucked from vivid dreams.

King Charles and Queen Camilla walked out of the TARDIS from the iconic British television show, Doctor Who. Source: Getty / Francois Nel

King Charles and Camilla arrive by TARDIS

One of the most unique scenes from Friday morning was the image of King Charles and Queen Camilla emerging from a very large TARDIS — the name for the time machine in the long-running British sci-fi television show, Doctor Who.

Gasps and cheers came from the crowd as the royal couple appeared on a stage that transformed into a magic garden.

Scotland's largest city welcomed able-bodied and para-athletes from 74 competing nations, including a third of Australia's 257-strong team who were part of the procession.

It's not the first time a monarch has appeared at a similar event. For the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics, Queen Elizabeth II appeared to skydive into the stadium alongside Daniel Craig, James Bond-style.

In Glasgow, the UK's new prime minister Andy Burnham was also in attendance, alongside Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and the First Minister of Wales Rhun ap Iorwerth.

Performers took to the stage during the opening on the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Source: Getty / James Fearn

A party — with unicorns

The opening ceremony traversed through many facets of Glasgow's history and culture, starting with a day in the life of the industrial city, pictured under its famous Glasgow Central Station clock.

The flashmob soon descended into a bizarre fever dream, where dancing unicorns with traffic cones paid tribute to the city's underground club culture.

Dancers wore bedazzled unicorns on their heads. Source: PA / Andrew Milligan

For decades, traffic cones have been regularly placed on an equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington and remain a symbol of Glaswegians' resistance to authority.

The unicorn is both a nod to the playful tradition and the creature being the national animal of Scotland since the 1300s.

Performers also donned large, shiny star costumes. Source: Getty / Francois Nel

There were also plenty of cameos and performances, including from a range of Scottish celebrities.

Former Doctor Who actor Sylvester McCoy made an appearance, as well as comedian Greg McHugh, cycling legend Sir Chris Hoy, and singers Callum Beattie, KT Tunstall, Tom Walker and Nathan Evans.

King Charles also met Finne, the unicorn mascot representing the 2026 Games. Source: Getty / Aaron Chown

King Charles even had the pleasure of meeting the official mascot for the 2026 Games — a unicorn named Finnie, with a traffic cone for a horn and a pink-and-purple mane.

Loch Ness Monsters and flaming teacakes

Victoria's withdrawal was also referenced throughout the night — with George Black, chair of the Glasgow 2026 organising committee, hailing Scotland's cultural capital for saving the games.

"A city built by people who believe that when something matters, you step forward," Black said on stage.

"When the future of these Games was uncertain, Glasgow didn't ask, 'can we?'

"We asked, "When do we get started?'"

The Loch Ness monster also attended the Glasgow ceremony. Source: Getty / Ross MacDonald

Even Nessie, the Loch Ness Monster, cleared up its schedule to make an appearance.

The creature appeared on a screen before being magically coaxed onto the stage by actor Sam Heughan of Outlander fame and a group of bagpipers.

The ceremony also featured a giant teacake, spurting with pyrotechnics. Source: PA / Andrew Milligan

The finale featured a giant teacake with pyrotechnics flowing from it, taking off from the centre of the stage.

It was a nod to the dancing Teacakes which appeared the last time Glasgow hosted the event in 2014.

Back then, dancers wore costumes representing dessert and national treasure, Tunnock's Tea Cakes — which is a Scottish treat of chocolate-covered marshmallows — and quickly became a worldwide hit.

At the time, a single teacake prop sold at official auctions for over $3,000.

Today's ceremony was held at the Hydro Arena in Glasgow, which fits about 15,000 people, and was the first time a Commonwealth Games opening ceremony was held indoors.

title: Not just phishing: The scams to watch for if you're an Origin Energy customer
text:
In brief As many as 4.8 million Origin Energy customers could be affected by a cyber attack that exposed personal data.

Experts have warned the fallout may go beyond phishing scams.

Nearly five million Australians have been urged to stay vigilant for scams after a cyber attack on Origin Energy saw customer data accessed and disclosed.

Origin — Australia's largest energy retailer, with roughly 4.8 million customer accounts across electricity, gas, LPG and internet services — confirmed that names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and account information were all potentially viewed in the breach.

It said on Thursday it was working to understand how many of its customers were affected.

Also potentially exposed were the last four digits of credit cards and the last three digits of bank accounts.

That combination of data has raised the risk of follow-up scams, particularly phishing attempts that use real account details to appear more convincing.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Phishing scams involve fraudsters posing as a trusted organisation, often via email or text, to trick people into handing over personal details, passwords, or banking information.

But experts warn phishing may not be the only thing customers need to worry about.

How Origin customers can protect themselves

New guidance from the company has urged customers to stay alert for scam emails and texts, designed to deceive people into providing their personal details.

"These fake emails often include a corporate logo and look like they've come from a legitimate company," Origin said.

Anyone who believes they've received a scam email is encouraged to report it to Scamwatch .

READ MORE Origin Energy reports customer bank, credit card details caught up in data breach

Origin has recommended customers keep a strong, unique password for their account and never share it with anyone, stressing it will never ask for a password over the phone or via email.

If a scam email arrives, the company's advice is to not click links, open attachments or forward it on, but to report it directly.

To tell a genuine email or text apart from a fake, Origin says to check for a suspicious sender address, spelling mistakes or bad grammar, and where any links actually lead.

"We've seen scam websites posing under originnergy.com.au so look carefully at the website address," Origin said, adding that the only safe way to pay a bill was via their website or the Origin app.

The company has also flagged fake job offers, and bogus calls or emails requesting orders or parts from people posing as Origin procurement staff, as scams to watch for.

Experts say Origin's response has fallen short

Some experts say the breach is another example of a major company failing to handle a data incident well, and are calling for tough accountability standards for essential service providers.

The breach represents the country's most high-profile cyber incident since Partnered Health, owned by private equity firm Quadrant, said earlier in July that its medical records were breached, affecting 21 of its clinics in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra.

In 2025, airline Qantas said it had customer data published by cybercriminals, while telco giant Optus and health insurer Medibank were hit in attacks in 2022 that sparked cyber-resilience laws.

READ MORE Australian patient details exposed in GP network cyberattack

"Companies must do better," Jacqueline Boaks from the Centre of Applied Ethics at Curtin University said.

"Delays in notifications, including reports that Origin ignored hackers' emails, passive language ('information may have been accessed') and minimising language (suggesting customers should be less worried about non-payment details being leaked) are extremely disappointing."

Rumpa Dasgupta, a lecturer in cybersecurity at La Trobe University, called it a "disappointing day" for Australian consumers and said concern extends beyond the leak of payment data.

"An electricity bill is more than just an invoice. It can provide valuable insights into a household," she said. "Energy consumption patterns may reveal when residents are typically home or away, the types of appliances they use, occupancy trends, and even periods of extended absence, such as weekends or holidays."

"In the wrong hands, this information could be exploited not only for highly targeted phishing campaigns but also to support physical crimes such as burglary by identifying vulnerable properties."

Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer in cybersecurity at UNSW, said it was "encouraging" to see Origin responding quickly, but that customers expect "robust measures" from a company operating critical infrastructure.

"Even if payment details were not compromised, personal information such as names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses can still be valuable to cybercriminals and may be used for targeted phishing, identity theft and social engineering attacks," Masood said.

"Incidents like this reinforce that cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue; it is a core part of operating essential services."

title: Trump's new Australian tariffs reveal complex truths, experts say as government urges repeal
text:
in brief US President Donald Trump has unveiled sweeping new international trade tariffs.

Australia is one of dozens of countries hit with a new 12.5 per cent levy on trade goods.

The government has hit back at blanket new 12.5 per cent tariffs imposed by the United States on Australian goods, which came into effect on Friday.

The new permanent levy replaces a temporary 10 per cent tariff due to expire at the same time and is part of what the US claims is an effort to tackle the global issue of "forced labour" in supply chains.

Whilst the government insists its handling of forced labour and modern slavery is top-tier, one expert has said Australia's protections are greatly lacking, while another has suggested that Australia is a victim of Trump's tensions with China in this scenario.

Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell has called for the tariff measures to be reversed, telling SBS News that they are "unjustified" and "inconsistent" with existing free-trade agreements with the US.

"These tariffs … should be removed," he said in a statement.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Australia's measures to combat forced labour and modern slavery are among the strongest in the world, and we are recognised globally, including in the US, for our leadership."

Almost all goods sent to the US will be affected at the specific direction of US President Donald Trump.

However, roughly 70 per cent of Australian exports are already covered under existing tariff exemptions, although it is not clear whether these exemptions will roll over under the new, higher rate.

SBS News has contacted the Office of the US Trade Representative for comment.

Australia has increased its exports to the United States by 67 per cent since April 2025, when a blanket 10 per cent global tariff was applied on Trump's so-called "Liberation Day", Farrell said.

Australia exported some $35.6 billion worth of goods to the United States in 2025, according to US COMTRADE data. Source: AAP / Darren England

Primary exports to the US include beef, gold, wine, medical products, and various mining resources, the volume of which has increased dramatically, Farrell said, bringing the total value of the trading relationship to $1.32 trillion.

"Our largest exports to the United States continue to get into the United States tariff-free. What are they? It's beef, it's gold, and it's copper," Farrell told a press conference on Friday.

Australia is among 41 other economies the US trade department claims have failed to "impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor". These include Brazil, China, Egypt, India, Israel, Japan, Norway, Russia, and Singapore.

Other regions, which the US claims have also failed to "enforce" forced labour prohibitions, face a 10 per cent tariff. These include Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Mexico.

The action is being taken against the US' 60 largest trading partners in an effort to "correct what is both a human rights abuse and a distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere".

The Australian Industry Group has described the tariffs as "both disappointing and meritless".

"Unfortunately, a tariff regime now appears to be the new normal when dealing with the United States and signals a further blow for Australian aspirations for a free and open global trading system," CEO Innes Willox said.

Justification under question

Trump has made tariffs central to his second term in office — arguing their use will deliver economic prosperity to the US — however, his previous attempt to impose them was struck down by the US Supreme Court in February, prompting the temporary 10 per cent levy.

Democrats in the US, like Linda Sánchez, have criticised the move as an "end-run" around the US Supreme Court to "reimpose his illegal tariffs".

Many experts have said the "forced labour" argument is something of a smokescreen.

Professor Lisa Toohey, international trade law expert at the University of New South Wales, told SBS News the European Union "has a more strict legal regime to prevent forced labour" than the US, and yet it is also subject to the new tariffs.

"The United States doesn't seem to be doing that much to address its own forced labour," she said. "The United States is one of a handful of countries where it has forced prison labour. Australia, by contrast, does not have forced prison labour."

She added that there is a perception these tariffs are "discriminatory" and there is no indication that the money raised will go toward addressing the issue of modern slavery.

Modern slavery a 'really serious' issue

Defence Minister Richard Marles has argued that the tariffs make "no sense".

While modern slavery is "definitely something which needs to be combated around the world", Australia has "among the strongest" laws globally to address it, Marles told ABC radio.

However, professor Justine Nolan, director of the Australian Human Rights Institute, told SBS News that Australia's Modern Slavery Act 2018 is "inadequate" to deal with the issue.

The framework requires companies with an annual revenue above $100 million to report on supply chain risks.

"They don't have to do anything about it," Nolan said. "There is no obligation to take action, and it doesn't have an effective enforcement framework, so no sanctions."

Earlier this month, Labor announced it would be reforming the act to include financial penalties for non-compliance and criminal sanctions for failing to prevent modern slavery.

Trade Minister Don Farrell (left) and Defence Minister Richard Marles (right) have both spoken out against the tariffs imposed by the United States. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

Those changes, Nolan argued, would put Australia "back into the world-leading category of tackling the issue", however Labor's lack of commitment to an import ban may result in US tariff measures being kept in place.

Countries paying just the 10 per cent tariff are those with forced labour import bans, the same mechanism used by the US, or ones that have committed to imposing one.

Some 50 million people around the world are estimated to be in modern slavery, with more than half of those in supply chains. In Australia, 40,000 people are thought to be living in modern slavery conditions, which includes both forced marriage and forced labour.

It's a "really serious global issue," Nolan said, and Australia has seen examples of it in the agricultural, cleaning, and construction sectors.

"There's mixed motivations for the US, and perhaps the instrument they're applying is blunter than would be useful, but if it also motivates countries like Australia to strengthen our legal approach and to strengthen regulation, then that's a useful thing," she added.

No going back

In the post-World War Two era, the US had been the global champion of free trade. Experts now warn this latest move represents another shift toward a more fractured, less cooperative world.

Nicholas Frank, international political economist at Monash University, told SBS News that the broader context is the ongoing economic rivalry between the US and China — smaller players like Australia are simply caught up in it.

These new tariffs, he argued, could be an attempt by the US to "kind of carve up global trade and reduce China's influence and role in the global economy".

"That's why they are so widespread: they're hitting everyone because everyone does business with China," he said.

Trump's tit-for-tat trade war with China last year saw the US impose 145 per cent tariffs on Chinese goods, with China retaliating at 125 per cent. The Asian superpower and Australia's largest trading partner has also been hit by the new 12.5 per cent charge.

Rivalry between the two nations continues to play out in dominance over energy and artificial intelligence, with trade simply being another front, Frank argued.

Having lost much of its manufacturing sector to Asia, the US may well force nations to "pick between the US and China", in an effort to pull back global trading power.

"There is a much larger story about what's actually happening to the global trade system and how," he said. "This is just a small piece of it."

title: Not a 'one off spike': Why higher petrol prices are set to return
text:
Key Points Oil prices are expected to rise as the government's reduction to the fuel excise is due to end next month.

Meanwhile, bonds traders ratcheted up expectations that the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates for a fourth time in 2026.

Petrol prices are expected to rise once again, which could cause a crunch at the bowser for Australians already feeling the pinch.

While Australia's resilient labour market continues to be a bright spot in the nation's economy, including the addition of more than 76,000 jobs in June, dark clouds are gathering on the horizon.

After the Australian Bureau of Statistics released another strong labour force report on Thursday, bonds traders ratcheted up expectations that the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates for a fourth time in 2026.

The market is now full priced in for a rate hike by Christmas. A few weeks ago it was a 50-50 bet.

title: Australia’s winter wonderland is becoming increasingly reliant on a backup plan
text:
In brief Australia recorded one its worst starts to a snow season in decades this year.

But some resorts were able to turn lifts on the opening weekend thanks to artificial snowmaking.

As the sun rises over Mount Buller in Victoria's High Country, the hum of snow guns echoes across the mountain, blanketing ski runs in artificial snow.

It's a scene that's becoming increasingly common at Australia's alpine resorts.

As winters become less predictable, operators are investing heavily in snowmaking technology, effectively an insurance policy keeping lifts turning and visitors coming when natural snowfall falls short.

With little natural snow falling until 3 July, one of the slowest starts to winter in decades, several resorts still managed to turn lifts on the traditional June long weekend opening thanks to artificial snowmaking — even if only thin stripes of beginner's terrain were open.

Among them was Mount Buller, which has invested $17 million in snowmaking in the past 25 years.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The resort now operates more than 300 snow guns across almost 80km of ski runs, which can generally operate only at a wet-bulb temperature of -2C or below.

Mount Buller also has five snow factories — shipping container-like buildings capable of producing snow around the clock, regardless of temperature.

Mount Buller has more than 300 snow guns, which produce artificial snow. Source: LightRocket / Ye Myo Khant

"Snowmaking has progressively become more and more significant around the world because it smooths out the variability from season to season," Mount Buller spokesperson Rhylla Morgan told SBS News.

"We haven't had many of those big snow events yet. There have only been a handful so far this season, so snowmaking helps us fill in those gaps.

"It allows us to maintain snow cover across the ski area and steadily build that base, which has enabled us to progressively open more terrain and keep our guests skiing and snowboarding."

Morgan said snowmaking technology — which is both water-and energy-intensive — had improved significantly in the decades since its introduction, allowing resorts to produce higher-quality snow more efficiently.

"The technology has really become very finessed; there are amazing companies around the world working to improve that every year," she said.

Resorts also rely on "snow farming" to extend their seasons by creating snow stockpiles in south-facing and shaded areas, which are then groomed to top up runs.

She said Australia's ski industry — which supports more than 22,000 jobs and contributes billions of dollars to the economy — was continuously adapting to the changing climate.

Why has this season been so slow?

While snowmaking has helped resorts cope with poor natural conditions, it hasn't changed the weather.

After an early July dump of snow, the Spencers Creek measuring site — considered the most reliable site for natural snow depth in NSW — recorded a depth of 68cm on 21 July. A good year would exceed a metre.

Experts say a combination of El Niño, the Southern Annular Mode and long-term climate change has contributed to this year's slow start to the snow season.

Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and Protect Our Winters science alliance member, said an intensified El Niño had brought more persistent high-pressure systems across south-eastern Australia.

"It's bringing a lot more of those big high-pressure systems that give the clear skies, which means less snow," he said.

The same weather pattern has also produced temperature inversions, where it can be warmer on mountain peaks than lower down the slopes.

Those conditions likely contributed to record July temperatures across Victoria's alpine resorts, with Mount Hotham reaching 12C and Falls Creek 11.5C last weekend — breaking their previous July records of 8.7C and 9.8C by several degrees.

Watkins, who is also an avid skier, said record-breaking temperatures were increasingly common in a warming climate.

"I don't think much surprises us as climate scientists anymore. I'd like to say I'm shocked by it, but I'm not," he said.

"The last decade, and even just this year, looking at what's happened in Europe, what's happened in the UK, and even what's happening in Canada and America right now, breaking records by two or three degrees is happening reasonably often."

Warmer conditions also mean cold fronts that might once have delivered snow are increasingly bringing rain instead, degrading the snow pack.

But the high-pressure systems can produce cold, dry nights — ideal conditions for snow guns.

"That's sort of a perfect scenario for snowmaking … which has been a saviour in many places," he said.

A 2024 report by the Australian Mountain Research Facility and Australian National University found snow cover had reduced by 30 per cent between 1954 and 2021, while the length of the ski season had contracted between 17 and 28 per cent at most resorts.

Despite the grim picture, Watkins said snowmaking would still be viable under a warming in the depths of winter.

"In the middle of the season, I think snowmaking has great potential," he said.

“[But] our seasons are still going to get shorter," he said.

As for this snow season, Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist Jonathan How said it would only take one big weather system to turn the fortunes around.

"We're entering the back end of winter, so certainly you know we could see some systems coming through still."

title: The US' $166 billion refund comes with a much bigger cost
text:
In brief Despite a Supreme Court ruling against him, Donald Trump uses tariffs to create a sustained economic uncertainty.

The cost of that uncertainty could lead to unforeseen changes to longstanding economic order.

An Australian clothing company, Nashie, recently received a six-figure refund from the US government, including 6 per cent interest, for tariffs it had paid on US imports. It’s just one of thousands of businesses reclaiming tariffs imposed on what President Donald Trump called "Liberation Day".

Of the roughly US$166 billion (AU$237 billion) due to be refunded, more than US$85 billion (AU$121 billion) has already been returned to businesses.

But while a US Supreme Court ruling in February reversed the tariffs, much of the economic and political damage, and perhaps some of the Trump administration’s gains, will be hard to undo.

Tariffs not designed to last

Trump’s April 2025 tariffs relied on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), a 1977 law that lets presidents respond to extraordinary foreign threats — yet never mentions the word "tariff".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

On 20 February 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled in a 6-3 decision that IEEPA did not authorise tariffs — under the Constitution, only Congress has the power to impose taxes and duties.

The decision placed an important limit on the president’s power to impose tariffs. But it did not end Trump’s tariff policy, which was, from the beginning, designed to buy time to rewrite US trade relations with the rest of the world.

Trump responded with a temporary 10 per cent global tariff, which expires on 24 July after the statutory 150-day limit.

Trump has also pursued more targeted tariffs under laws dealing with unfair trade practices, national security and anti-slavery claims.

These require investigations into foreign trade practices and lengthy procedures, which slow the process and also create a record that can be scrutinised in court.

The US Trade Representative’s findings on alleged forced labour have prepared the ground for a 12.5 per cent tariff on exports from 54 countries, including Australia, China, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, starting on 24 July 2026.

So while the Supreme Court closed one legal door, the Trump administration was already preparing to walk through another. And it has bought itself yet more time.

The fiscal cost for the US

The refunds paid out contributed to a US$120 billion (AU$171 billion) federal deficit this June, in sharp contrast to the US$27 billion (AU$38 billion) surplus in June 2025.

That said, the US$166 billion (AU$236 billion) being paid out is not a fine. Much of it is money the government collected without legal authority and must now return. This is real money, but it’s less than 2 per cent of the projected 2026 federal government spending.

Without any fanfare to match "Liberation Day", the political cost may be smaller still.

The refunds involve a technical process and are dispersed among many importers, making them far less visible than the original tariff announcements.

And concessions that trading partners, including the UK and the European Union, made under the threat of higher tariffs don’t automatically vanish when a tariff is struck down.

What’s in a refund?

For businesses, repaying money they should never have paid doesn’t recreate the position they were in before the tariffs.

Importers had capital tied up for months as financing costs mounted, orders were cancelled, and inventory sat stranded. Many had to renegotiate contracts.

They paid customs brokers and lawyers, and delayed other investments while waiting to learn which tariff would apply. Some stopped shipping to the US altogether, unsure what customs duties they would incur.

Smaller firms were especially exposed. They generally have smaller cash reserves, fewer alternative suppliers, and less capacity to absorb an unexpected increase in duty.

One analysis estimated small business importers in the US each paid US$306,000 extra in tariffs on average.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta estimates that "financially constrained" businesses will receive 34 per cent of all refunds, or about US$56 billion. These firms are most likely to use the money to invest, hire staff or reduce prices.

Better-financed businesses are more likely to save it, repay debt or distribute it to shareholders. PepsiCo said it would use the refunds to offset some commodity inflation.

But few are likely to pass the refunds back to consumers due to the complexity and cost involved. Nintendo is being sued by its own customers, who argue the tariff refunds should be paid to consumers to offset the higher prices they paid.

Access is also uneven. A business with a US bank account and customs broker can get its refund relatively smoothly. Australian businesses shipping via Australia Post face further delays: those shipments weren’t entered through the system US Customs and Border Protection uses for refunds, and no refund pathway exists yet.

Nor does the refund necessarily reach whoever ultimately paid. Rather, it goes to the importer, even where the cost was passed on to a retailer or consumer through higher prices.

The deeper cost is uncertainty

The most important consequence of Trump’s tariff policy is persistent uncertainty.

Trump can impose an immediate commercial disruption, then use that disruption as leverage in negotiations with other governments. The latest example is Monday’s 50 per cent tariff on a range of Canadian goods, which the US says responds to Canadian retaliation and discrimination against US cars, dairy and alcohol.

Persistent uncertainty also encourages global commerce to fragment into competing blocs whose market access is more predictable.

READ MORE What Trump's 100 per cent pharmaceutical tariff means for Australia

As our Weaponised Trade project shows, the greater danger is other governments adopting the same playbook: temporary, legally questionable trade restrictions becoming the norm rather than the exception.

Litigation to roll back these measures takes months or even years.

And if a court does eventually invalidate a measure, the US can invoke another law and restart the process. Courts operate retrospectively. Markets, on the other hand, react to them immediately.

The Supreme Court ruling did not return lost customers, reverse commercial decisions or restore confidence in predictable trade rules.

Tariffs can be refunded. Uncertainty cannot.

Markus Wagner is Professor of Law at the University of Wollongong School of Law.

But the tribunal determined the scoring change was invalid and against EA’s own rules, concluding that the grand prix champion should have been calculated with the percentage-based model typically deployed in dressage, where horses are judged on their movements during a routine. On that basis, Estupendo and McKinnon would have had the edge. Reacting to the tribunal’s ruling, state organisations Equestrian NSW and Dressage NSW said the championship rug for 2024 would be presented again next month at their awards night. “The decision provides important clarity regarding the application of the rules and reinforces the importance of fairness, consistency and transparency across our sport,” they said. “We extend our sincere congratulations to Viv Lipshut, David McKinnon and Estupendo on being recognised as the 2024 Australian grand prix champion. This is a significant achievement and one that deserves to be celebrated.”

Advertisement

Lipshut, who herself stopped riding after having a stroke in 2017, has accepted an invitation to attend the NSW awards dinner. Related Article Investigation

Equestrian Scoring feud, intimidation claim engulfs Olympics’ most expensive sport But after encountering resistance from national-level officials from the moment she questioned the outcome of the blue riband event, she said the battle had taken its toll. EA opposed the matter being sent to the Australian government’s independent sports umpire, but the tribunal accepted it after an investigation by this masthead. “Although I am grateful this matter has now been resolved, the nearly two-year struggle has come at a considerable personal cost to my health and wellbeing,” Lipshut said.

Advertisement

“My sincere hope is that this determination will help ensure that no member of Equestrian Australia ever has to endure such a prolonged struggle again simply to have their concerns heard.” Equestrian Australia, which will receive $5.7 million in federal funding in 2026-27 via the Australian Sports Commission, has also been embroiled in a legal dispute with its former digital services provider. It has vowed to vigorously defend separate proceedings brought against it by former Olympian Heath Ryan in the NSW Supreme Court. Ryan’s EA membership has been provisionally suspended for more than a year while the International Federation for Equestrian Sports investigates a video that showed him whipping a horse 42 times. Updated WorldEuropeBushfires Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as more than 200,000 people flee flames in France, Spain Caroline Blumberg , Samuel Petrequin and Joseph Wilson Updated July 26, 2026 — 12:44pm ,first published July 25, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Bordeaux/Madrid: Wildfires on the coast of south-western France moved inland towards Bordeaux on Saturday (Paris time), forcing the evacuation of thousands in the city’s suburbs, while blazes over the border in Spain claimed a life. Hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated in both countries. The fires are the latest natural disasters linked to sustained dry spells and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. From a beach in Arcachon, locals and holidaymakers watch in astonishment as the fire rages on the other side of the bay, in Lège-Cap-Ferret. Hans Lucas via AFP “The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X. So far this month, temperatures have averaged 32.2 degrees in the region of France hit by the fires, which is 7.3 degrees above the average July peak between 1961 and 1990, according to data on Reuters Climate Monitor.

Advertisement

“We expect a fight that will be long and very difficult,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters. France’s armed forces have been drafted in to help overwhelmed fire brigades. On Saturday afternoon, an A400M military transport, the largest aircraft in France’s fleet, joined the effort by dumping liquid over a flame-hit forest, as shown in Reuters TV footage filmed from a helicopter. People pose on the beach in Andernos-Les Bains as a fire burns to its north in Lege Cap-Ferret forest, in south-western France. AFP Organisers of the Tour de France announced a truncated 21st and final stage of the famed sporting event, in part to ease the strain on emergency services. In France, as in Spain, smoke billowed from the advancing wall of flames, leaving charred homes in its wake. Three blazes near Madrid, two of which merged on Friday, have prompted Spain to declare its first national emergency over a wildfire.

Advertisement

A far smaller brush fire near coastal Valencia, which began and was extinguished on Saturday, caused the death of an elderly man in his car, the interior ministry said. Spain’s Civil Protection Service said it expected four more water-dumping aircraft to arrive on Saturday, two from Italy and two from Greece – sent as part of a European Union response. Firefighting aircraft from the Netherlands and Portugal have already been deployed. People leave their homes after wildfires in the area forced thousands of tourists to evacuate in Arcachon, France. Getty Images The spreading fires have burned more than 3400 hectares of forest in south-western France. Getty Images High winds have stoked and spread the fires in both countries. The coast near wine region Bordeaux is a tourist hotspot that includes pine forests that can catch fire easily.

Advertisement

Roughly 197,000 people have so far been evacuated from the adjacent Gironde and Landes departments since wildfires broke out last week. In Spain, roughly 88,000 people have been evacuated or confined to their homes because of the three major fires. French minister Nunez said the flames were about 30 kilometres from Bordeaux. The government has warned against road or rail travel to the area. Bordeaux airport remained open, but its website reported train and bus links were affected. “I left without any of my things, with nothing, with the two little children,” 71-year-old Bernadette said of her grandsons after abandoning her house on the coast in the middle of the night. She was speaking at a large conference centre in Bordeaux converted into emergency accommodation. “I forgot plenty of things, my eye medications, everything.”

Advertisement

Many Madrid residents have second homes in the area west of the capital where the two fires merged, which is still in the administrative region of Madrid. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready A third fire in Avila province has threatened to merge with the two in Madrid. Further complicating efforts to control them, one firefighters’ union in Madrid is on strike, although the effect on numbers of firefighters deployed appeared small. Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia reiterated a warning against outdoor activities in Madrid because of the smoke. “Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” she said on X.

Advertisement

Those evacuated near Madrid gave similar accounts of hurried departures to those who sought shelter in Bordeaux. Related Article Heatwave Australia’s used to heatwaves. What makes Europe’s ‘heat dome’ different? “I saw clouds of smoke rising into the sky. That’s when I realised something was happening,” Rodika, 60, from the small town of Fresnedillas de La Oliva, told Reuters. “I think we all panicked. Then we received the message telling us to get ready, take whatever valuables we could, whatever was most important. title: Music Review: Laufey proves jazz music can be cool among Gen Z
text:
