NationalWAReview Music Review: Laufey proves jazz music can be cool among Gen Z Indigo Lemay-Conway July 26, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Concert

Laufey

RAC Arena, July 26, 2026

★★★★★

Jazz music is having a revival and has brought with it a new young generation of followers. Thousands of Gen Z fans packed into RAC Arena on Saturday night to see Icelandic singer Laufey perform her A Matter of Time tour – and she did not disappoint. Laufey (pronounced loy-vay) kicked off the Australian and New Zealand leg of her tour in Perth, telling the sold-out crowd she wanted to make the journey to the west coast because she knew what it felt like to live in a place artists rarely visited. Laufey performed at RAC Arena on July 26, 2026. Nicole Mago Foundations Music

Advertisement

“Don’t worry, you guys. I’m from the middle of nowhere. I hope you understand,” she said with a laugh. “So I always feel like I need to go to the places that are far away because I can remember every single artist who came to Iceland growing up, and it was like the most random assortment of artists and I just always felt so seen. “So I just want to thank you so much for inviting me to your country and to your city … you sold this place out, this is crazy there are so many of you here. I really can’t believe my life lately.” The classically trained musician began the show with a selection of her best known hits like Lover Girl, Falling Behind and Too Little Too Late with a live ensemble and four dancers by her side. The castle backdrop, lighting and projections all added to Laufey’s whimsical energy, creating an ambience that felt like something from an old Disney movie.

Advertisement

As an audience member – who is somewhere between a millennial and Gen Z – it was surprising to see how many young people resonated with her older style of music. The show was split into four acts and an encore, and had one act dedicated entirely to jazz. Laufey kicked off her Australian and New Zealand tour in Perth on Saturday night. Nicole Mago Foundations Music Opting to re-invent a handful of songs as jazz pieces, Laufey performed with a stripped back band in a bid to “nerd out” and make the room feel intimate. “With this tour, I really want to find a way to make these very big rooms feel cosy, and I also wanted the opportunity to just nerd out and take some of my older songs and put them in new costumes, rearrange them,” she said.

Advertisement

“So if you’re trying to keep up, and you feel like the beat’s a little funky, it’s a little funky on purpose.” Whether it was because the 28-year-old comes across as a youthful ray of sunshine, or because her music genuinely speaks to people in a way that modern music seems to be lacking, one thing was certain – the younger generation loved it. Two outfit changes later and the performer closed her show with a song called Letter to My 13 Year Old Self. The song was a reminder to never let anyone stop you from becoming who you want to be. In the words overheard by two teens at the end of the song: “I really needed to hear that today.” Pop music isn’t going anywhere, but Laufey is a great reminder that individuality has the power to resonate with people and sell out arenas too.

title: ‘The new LA’: How capital of K-pop catapulted Queensland dancers to stardom
text:
World Street Woman Fighter was broadcast across the globe.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kaea Pearce has danced alongside Jennifer Lopez at the 2020 Super Bowl and stars in Justin Bieber’s Sorry music video, which has been watched more than 3.9 billion times on YouTube. But ask the New Zealand-born, Gold Coast-based performer about the greatest experience of her career so far, and she’ll tell you it was competing on a South Korean dance-battle reality show. “I think it’s the new LA,” Pearce says of South Korea. Last year, she was approached to lead the squad representing Australia on the show World of Street Woman Fighter, a dance competition against all-women teams from the US, South Korea, Japan and New Zealand. Kaea Pearce (right) handpicked the group of dancers who represented Australia. Pearce had just one week to form the AG Squad – a crew of dancers that would be catapulted to stardom among South Korean fans. Her team came second, beaten only by Japan’s Osaka Ojo Gang.

Advertisement

For Pearce, it was the best job she’d ever done. “We were able to be the stars and show the world we aren’t just back-up dancers – we’re artists,” she said. The AG Squad spent time touring South Korea and meeting fans. Instagram @agsquadofficial Brisbane dancer and choreographer Danica McKenzie, also in the AG Squad, was left just as awestruck after her first experience in K-pop. She said South Korean viewers treated the AG Squad like celebrities when they toured after the show aired. “It’s otherworldly,” she said. “Usually [dancers] go to a concert backing up for an artist. No one is there for you. It was insane to know that in Korea as a dancer, you are an artist. You’re an idol to them.”

Advertisement

The Australian dance squad now has a large following in South Korea. Dominique Falla, an associate professor at Griffith University and the author of The K-Pop Content Strategy, said Seoul had become one of the world’s most important centres for commercial choreography. And she agreed that the South Korean attitude towards dancers was hugely different to that in Australia. “[In Australia] you’re a back-up dancer, a body in a music video, and your name rarely appears anywhere,” she said. “There’s very little pathway from skilled dancer to recognised artist.” In South Korea, however, the pop industry places choreography at the centre of musical performance. Dancers “are presented as artists and competitors in their own right”. “The Korean entertainment industry invests in dancers in a way the West simply doesn’t,” Falla said.

Advertisement

The AG Squad in Seoul, South Korea. But while programs such as World of Street Woman Fighter delivered fame to their contestants, Falla warned that sometimes the work was precarious. “Dancers and choreographers can still experience insecure freelance work, demanding schedules, limited bargaining power, and difficulties receiving appropriate credit or ownership of choreography,” Falla said. Danica McKenzie is a performer and choreographer based in Brisbane. McKenzie is a champion for Brisbane’s dance scene, teaching at Mad Dance House in the Brisbane CBD and The Home Base in Darra. But she said she could understand why performers often flocked to Sydney and Melbourne – or further afield – to advance their careers. “There’s minimal opportunities for performers in Brisbane, which I guess is why so many dancers are moving out of Brisbane,” McKenzie said.

Australians may soon struggle to take advantage of free travel insurance policies offered by their premium credit cards, travel agents have warned, as an imminent surcharge ban looks set to hit the generosity of cardholder perks and rewards schemes. The warning from travel agents about the consequences stemming from the reform to Australia’s payments system comes days after ANZ joined NAB and other banks that announced scaled-back credit card rewards programs and complimentary lounge access ahead of the ban on surcharges that have funded benefits and bonus offerings, coming into effect from October 1. Loading The Reserve Bank’s changes are aimed at making card payments fairer as cash usage declines, and are expected to cut banks’ revenue by $660 million a year by lowering caps on “intercharge fees”, which are paid by merchants every time a shopper pays for something with a card. Much of the travel-related coverage of the ban has centred on how it will likely become more difficult to accrue Qantas frequent flyer and other airline points and how bonus point sign-up incentives and earn rates on spending will diminish.

This is especially true of airfares, with Waddington saying commissions tend to be between 0 and 1 per cent. “Selling an airfare with little or zero commission means a customer’s credit card payment can see us face a loss for selling that airfare,” said Waddington, who has worked in the industry for more than 20 years.

While Encounter’s main focus is arranging groups of solo-travellers, Waddington said smaller agencies, which rely entirely on selling other providers’ tours, airfares and third-party products, are in a tough position. As such, Waddington is now considering refusing credit card payments from some customers. Encounter Travel director, travel agent Justine Waddington. “The alternative is that the customer pays by direct deposit, but where some bookings are time-sensitive, waiting for funds to clear can mean the deal vanishes for the traveller.” Only accepting debit “may be my only viable option”, Waddington said. “Just as a customer wants to avoid that fee, so does a business. So why is it reasonable that a business should have to absorb the same cost?”

To activate the policy, banks often require a minimum credit-card spend – often $500 – on a holiday-related expense before departure. While the extent of reliance on free travel insurance from their credit cards is unclear, an estimate based on survey data from Money.com.au last year was that 39 per cent of Australians rely on such policies and don’t take out extra paid policies. “Paying credit is the most convenient option for a customer. Not only could this mean they can’t pay on credit, can’t earn points on the dollars they spend on their holiday bookings ... but the ability to activate a complimentary travel insurance policy may disappear.”

Australian Travel Industry Association CEO Dean Long. “Agents are relying on slim margins, and they’re not the ultimate holder of these (travel) products,” he said. “Surcharging has allowed them to recoup their costs while maintaining customer perks.” “Australians seem to love rewards, and we do strange things for reward points, but this will be a change in the way we think about reward points, how we spend them, and how it changes consumer behaviour because you’ll see fewer points and less ability to claim benefits such as (travel) insurance,” Long said. title: UK expat 'has a bone to pick with Australia' over parking rule: 'Explain it'
text:
A travelling Brit has made an interesting observation about the parking habits of drivers in Australia, something he says is far from the norm in the UK.

Bobby Louth, who is travelling the country, said he's "got a bone to pick" with Aussies about how cars park on the street — they all tend to face the same direction.

"Can someone please explain it to me?" the English visitor asked this week online.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

He joked that the Australian approach has at times made it "an absolute nightmare to find a park".

Speaking to Yahoo News, Bobby said he's primarily "noticed it in the busy and built-up areas in the city" but, interestingly, "it hasn't stood out as much elsewhere". He shared pictures of cars parked in Sydney.

The difference left him wondering: "What is the need for that — what is the reasoning?"

"You've got to go to the end of the road, turn around, and then go in it," he said.

Bobby said the rule is much more noticeable in Aussie cities, and something he's not used to at home. (Tiktok/@bobbylouth63Bo)

What's behind this parking quirk in Australia?

In many parts of Australia, drivers are required to park in the same direction as traffic is travelling. The idea is mainly for safety.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Cars are easier to see at night because reflectors and lights face approaching traffic correctly, and it avoids vehicles pulling out into the flow of traffic.

However, enforcement and signage can vary between states and councils, and the rule applies to the direction of travel, not necessarily that every car on a street must face the same way.

The reason Bobby noticed it is that in many UK areas, drivers are more accustomed to parking in either direction where permitted.

Last year, another British man was caught by surprise, copping a $272 fine for parking the wrong way in Sydney.

His white Suzuki was nose-to-nose with the car parked next to him.

"Parking on the wrong side of the road is never a good idea, particularly at night when visibility is reduced," she said.

title: Sight Aussie skiers have been waiting for
text:
Crowds have descended on Australia's ski resorts as snowfall and cool temperatures bring a small reprieve to a bleak season, though snow-making conditions are not tipped to last long.

A busy Sunday on the ski fields follows what was the coldest day of the year for many to start the weekend.

Glen Innes Airport in the NSW Northern Tablelands plunged to -5.8C overnight, Weatherzone data shows, while at 9.30am Sunday Thredbo was still -1.3C.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Skiers were quick to hit the slopes at Thredbo on Sunday, as they were at nearby Perisher.

Australian snowboarding influencer Rani Siregar posted on Sunday that people were enjoying the conditions amid a lean season.

The ski fields at Thredbo were busy too on Sunday.

"No sugar-coating it, this is one of the worst seasons we've had in a long time. But you don't get to pick the conditions, you just gotta make the best of what you got," she said.

On the ground at Thredbo, one of the ski resort's staff says there was some enjoyable fresh snow on some of the resort's unmarked runs on Saturday, though that snow had hardened on Sunday.

"We have a couple of fine days on the way before the next storm crosses on Tuesday and Wednesday … The cloud up high should clear for a mainly sunny Sunday, enjoy it and have a good day," the staffer wrote in a daily weather report.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Australia's ski resorts have had a lean year so far, with an unseasonably warm May and June crippling much of the start of the season.

Images of one narrow man-made ski run at Victoria's Mt Buller last month created much chatter online, as most of the resort's alpine landscape was exposed grass and mud.

It has made the past week's snowfall a welcome reprieve.

Perisher has received 2cm of snowfall in the past seven days, and the carpark up Kosciuszko Road is full on Sunday morning. The live cameras show Mt Buller is busy too now the slopes have been coated in snow.

The Bureau of Meteorology's Angus Hines told NewsWire that warm conditions up at the ski resorts would melt the snow though.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"There hasn't been any fresh snow today or yesterday, sort of a little late last week," he said.

Perisher saw a good dump of snow for the Kings Birthday long weekend in early June.

"But it's not ideal snow making conditions either because it's actually tending pretty mild on the mountains today. We're looking at high temperatures … between three and six degrees on a lot of the alpine slopes.

"So just a little bit warm to really try and either make snow or keep the snow that's there."

Elsewhere conditions were "pretty benign", Mr Hines said.

The country was "in between" weather systems that brought a powerful cold front and low snowfall to Tasmania late last week, but a bit of that rainfall was still causing minor flooding.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Most of the country's had pretty mild weather, although, having said that, it has been very cold through the last couple of nights in northern New South Wales and southern Queensland … temperatures deeply into the negatives in some of those places."

A "fairly feeble" cold front hitting southern WA will gather momentum as it heads east in the coming days.

"It will pick up a bit of steam by the time it reaches Tasmania on Tuesday, so we're looking at another pretty strong wintry blast down in the very far south on Tuesday," Mr Hines said.

"Melbourne will get a little taste of that on Tuesday with some rain and then some cooler temperatures as we head into Wednesday.

"Sydney should have a pretty bright week for the most part, maybe tending showery towards the end of the week, but plenty of sunny days before that happens."
